1:1.t: Already at the very end of autumn our brother, your son the monk Sisinnius, delivered to me a letter from your Grace; on reading it I rejoiced that you are safe and well, and mindful of me and of all the brothers who serve the Lord in the holy places, in whose relief you make friends for yourself of the unrighteous mammon and prepare eternal tabernacles, so that you can say with David: How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of powers; my soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord. For if the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself where it may lay its young, why should you, who are a high priest of the Lord, and tread the winepresses at the end of the world so as to give to thirsting peoples the wine of the blood of Christ, not freely cry out and say: My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God; blessed are those who dwell in your house. […]

In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying. LXX: In the eighth month of the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying. That in the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes the seventieth year of the desolation of the temple, which had been foretold by Jeremiah, was completed, Zechariah himself is witness, saying: O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, with which you are angry? Behold, this is the seventieth year; and no one doubts that Cyrus, king of the Persians, who destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans, in the first year of his reign sent back from Babylon into Judea about fifty thousand captives; […]

1:2.t: The Lord was angry with your fathers in anger, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will turn to you, says the Lord of hosts; be not like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried, saying. LXX: The Lord was angry with your fathers with great wrath, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn to me, says the Lord of powers, and I will turn to you, says the Lord of powers; and do not become like your fathers, whom the prophets who were before rebuked, saying. The wrath of the Lord does not signify a disturbance in him who is angry, but the deserts and sins of those against whom the wrath of God rages; for the rest, the Lord never takes vengeance in anger, but rebukes in order to amend. Hence the prophet also prays in the psalms: O Lord, do not reprove me in your fury, nor rebuke me in your wrath, and in another place we read: Rebuke us, O Lord, yet not in your fury, but in mercy. […]

1:3.t: But not all who see are equally enlightened by Christ, but each is enlightened according to that measure by which he is able to receive the force of the light. And just as the eyes of our body are not equally enlightened by the sun, but the higher one ascends into lofty places and beholds its rising by the gazing of a more elevated watchtower, so much the more will he receive both of its splendor and its heat; so also our mind, the more loftily and highly it approaches Christ and presents itself nearer to the splendor of his light, so much the more magnificently and clearly will it be irradiated by his light, as he himself also says through the prophet: "Draw near to me, and I will draw near to you, says the Lord." And again he says: "I am a God drawing near, and not a God from afar."

And although he was angry with them, it is to you that the Lord of hosts speaks, for which Sabaoth is set down in the Hebrew, which the Seventy sometimes translated 'Almighty', sometimes 'of powers'. And he says: Turn to me, and I will turn to you, according to what we read: Draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you. To which this is the contrary: You have withdrawn from me, and I have withdrawn from you. Now he commands those who have returned from Babylon to return to the Lord, so that the Lord too may return to them, lest the sons begin to suffer what their fathers once suffered, to whom the prophets of that time likewise spoke. It is to be noted that in a few short verses and brief sentences, in Haggai and Zechariah, says the Lord of hosts is always added, so that they may know that it is God who commands, both against the command of the king and against the enemies raging round about; and that by this confidence they may be roused to the building of the temple.

When God says, "Turn ye unto me, and I will turn unto you," one of these clauses—that which invites our return to God—evidently belongs to our will; while the other, which promises His return to us, belongs to His grace. Here, possibly, the Pelagians think they have a justification for their opinion which they so prominently advance, that God's grace is given according to our merits. In the East, indeed, that is to say, in the province of Palestine, in which is the city of Jerusalem, Pelagius, when examined in person by the bishop, did not venture to affirm this. For it happened that among the objections which were brought up against him, this in particular was objected, that he maintained that the grace of God was given according to our merits,—an opinion which was so diverse from catholic doctrine, and so hostile to the grace of Christ, that unless he had anathematized it, as laid to his charge, he himself must have been anathematized on its account. […]
1:3.s: On Grace and Free Will, Chapter 10

1:4.t: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn from your evil ways, and from your most wicked thoughts; and they did not hear, nor did they attend to me, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn from your most wicked ways, and from your evil devices, and they did not attend so as to hear me, says the Lord. The sentence hangs on what precedes, and what follows must be fitted to what came before. For Zechariah is not speaking to the people, but is showing what the former prophets said to their fathers, to whom they cried, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn from your evil ways and from your most wicked thoughts. This is what Isaiah cried, this Hosea and Joel, Amos and Jeremiah: that they should forsake their evil ways and abandon their most wicked thoughts, by which they were sinning both in deed and in mind; […]

1:5.t: Your fathers, where are they, and the prophets? Will they live forever? But my words and my ordinances, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? And they turned and said: As the Lord of hosts purposed to do to us according to our ways and according to our devices, he has done to us. LXX: Your fathers, where are they, and the prophets? Will they live forever? But receive my words and my ordinances, which I command in my spirit to my servants the prophets, who overtook your fathers. And they answered and said: As the Lord Almighty was prepared to do to us according to our ways and according to our devices, so he has done to us. Where, he says, are your fathers, who did not hear me nor attend to me? Where are your prophets? For it is to be understood Ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (from the shared word): Your fathers, where are they, and your prophets, where are they? that is, the false prophets; for he would never say of the holy prophets: Will they live forever? 1:7.t: On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying. LXX: On the twenty-fourth, in the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat, in the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying. Some put the twelfth month in place of the eleventh, and, interpreting the twenty-fourth day of that month by arithmetical reckonings, suppose it to be a square, firm and stable number, wishing the things that are written to be certain and stable. But let us say that in the same second year of King Darius, in the third month after the first vision, that is, in the eleventh after the eighth, which among the Hebrews is called Shebat, the word of the Lord came again to Zechariah. That the second number is unclean, and pertains to the union of the flesh, and to the things of the world and of matter, we have often taught. […]

1:8.t:
And you will understand the sentence that follows if you compare with it these words in Zechariah:

"8. I saw the night, and behold a man sitting on a bay horse, and he stood in the midst of the shady mountains."

I believe this rider on the bay horse who stands in the midst of the shady mountains to be the same person mentioned in the prophecy before us, which says that the Holy One will come from a thick and shady mountain.

In each passage shady mountains are mentioned, and I believe they refer to the Paradise of God, which He planted eastward in Eden, or perhaps to the Heavenly Jerusalem. For "there are mountains around it, and the Lord is in the midst of his people." And these mountains are said to be shady, because they are full of divine powers and holy spirits, as of trees planted there and far-spreading. But in Zechariah clearly the vision was of a man riding on a bay horse, by which the Incarnation of our Saviour was meant, and the flesh in which He rode: while here "God a Holy One" is named. […]
1:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 15

1:8.t: [Daniel 7:5] "And behold another beast like a bear stood up on one side; and there were three rows in his mouth and in his teeth; and they said to him: 'Arise up and devour flesh in abundance.'" The second beast resembling a bear is the same as that of which we read in the vision of the statue (2:32): "His chest and arms were of silver." In the former case the comparison was based on the hardness of the metal, in this case on the ferocity of the bear. For the Persian kingdom followed a rigorous and frugal manner of life after the manner of the Spartans, and that too to such an extent that they used to use salt and nasturtium-cress in their relish. Let us consult the record of the childhood of Cyrus the Great (i.e., "The Education or Training" of Cyrus). And as for the fact that the bear is said to have "stood up on one side," the Hebrews interpret it by saying that the Persians never perpetrated any cruelty against Israel. Hence they are described in the Prophecy of Zechariah also as white horses (Zechariah 1:7-11). […]
1:8.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER SEVEN

1:8.t: I saw by night, and behold, a man mounting a red horse, and he was standing among the myrtle groves that were in the deep, and behind him horses red, dappled and white. And I said: What are these, my lord? And the angel who was speaking in me said to me: I will show you what these are. And the man who was standing among the myrtle groves answered and said: These are they whom the Lord has sent to walk through the earth. And they answered the angel of the Lord, who was standing among the myrtle groves, and said: We have walked through the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest. And the angel of the Lord answered and said: O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, with which you are angry? This is the seventieth year. And the Lord answered the angel who was speaking in me good words, words of consolation. […]

But the teachers of the churches understand the night in which the vision is seen as the obscurity of a mystical vision. For God made darkness his hiding place. And according to the Seventy translators it is said of him: The abyss like a garment is his clothing. Now the man who was mounting the red horse is the Lord and Savior, who, taking it up for the dispensation of our flesh, hears in Isaiah: Why are your garments red? He who is now shown as red to the captive people is described in the Apocalypse of John as sitting in white garments and on a white horse. And as to his being said to stand between two shady mountains — although 'two' is not found in the Hebrew — they take them as the New and the Old Testament, which is said to be covered with very dense foliage, and grove, and shady woods, because it is wrapped in many obscurities. And the myrtle groves that were in the deep, among which he is described as standing, they understand as the angelic powers, which ministered to him even when he was set in the flesh. […]

1:9.t: You see that God speaks not in the ears but in the heart; just as Zechariah too says: "And the angel who spoke within me said to me." There the angel is understood to be our Lord, who announces the will of the Father, who in Isaiah is called the "angel of great counsel."

So when the prophet saw a man mounting a red horse, and behind him red, dappled and white horses, and did not know what he had seen, and desired to know the meaning of his vision, and said: What are these, my lord? the angel who was speaking in him promises that he will tell; and while he keeps silent, the man who was standing among the myrtle groves relates it. These are the kingdoms which the Lord commanded to walk through the earth and to subject it to their power.

Then the prophet questions the same man and angel who was standing among the myrtle groves, and says: What are these, my lord? And the angel who was speaking in him, namely the prophetic sense, promises that he will show what he sees. And when he has promised, it is not he himself who answered, but another who was standing among the myrtle groves, and he says: These are they whom the Lord has sent to walk through the earth. For the apostles were sent by the Lord to fill the whole world with the preaching of the Gospel; and after they had fulfilled the work, they returned to the angel of great counsel who was standing among them (they who said with the Apostle: We are the good odor of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing) and among the peoples of both callings. And they said to him: We have walked through the earth, we have fulfilled the work enjoined on us, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest, which before was deserted by God; […]

Likewise, who will tell with what bodies angels appear to people, in such fashion as not to be visible but to be tangible? And again how, not through tangible corporeality but by spiritual power, angels produce certain visions, not to the eyes of the body but to those of the spirit or the mind, or can utter speech, not of the ear from without, but within the soul of humans, being themselves placed there, as is written in the book of the prophets: "And the angel that spoke in me said to me" (for what the prophet says is not "that spoke to me," but "in me").… They appear also in sleep and speak through dreams (for we read in the Gospel: "Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying"). These methods of communication tend to show that the angels have intangible bodies, and make it a very difficult question how the patriarchs could wash the feet of angels, and how Jacob could wrestle with an angel in contact so unmistakable. […]

1:11.t: In short, the angels who presided over the kingdoms and nations come not to another, but to the man himself and angel of the Lord who was standing among the myrtle groves, and say: We have walked through the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest. And the sense is: All the kingdoms under us are safe and pacified, and are not oppressed by any distress.

1:12.t: And if you reckon the period of the seven and sixty-two weeks in another way a third time, they will comprise 483 years, up to Augustus and Herod, the first king of foreign stock, in whose reign the Birth of our Saviour Jesus Christ is recorded to have occurred, if you begin to reckon from Darius and the completion of the Temple. For the prophet Zechariah shews that the seventy years of the Desolation of Jerusalem were completed in the second year of Darius, when he says: "On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month (this is the Sabbath), in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Barachiah." And then he adds, "And the Angel of the Lord answered, and said, O Almighty Lord, how long wilt thou not pity Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, which thou hast despised these seventy years past?" […]
1:12.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 2

1:12.t: [Daniel 5:2] "Being now drunken, he therefore gave order that the golden and silver vessels be brought in which his father, Nebuchadnezzar, had taken away from the temple which was in Jerusalem, in order that the king might drink from them..." The Hebrews hand down some such story as this: that up until the seventieth year, on which Jeremiah had said (Jeremiah 25:11) that the captivity of the Jewish people would be released (a matter of which Zechariah also speaks [Zechariah 1:12] in the first part of his book), Belshazzar had esteemed God's promise to be of none effect; therefore he turned the failure of the promise into an occasion of joy and arranged a great banquet, scoffing somewhat at the expectation of the Jews and at the vessels of the Temple of God. Punishment, however, immediately ensued. […]
1:12.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FIVE

1:12.t: From this answer the angel who interceded for Israel, taking the occasion to pray for the people, also says to the Lord: Since the whole world is quiet and at peace, why, O Lord, will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, especially since, according to your promises, the time of the captivity has been fulfilled?

And as to the plea, full of mercy, that, with the seventieth year at hand, God should have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, they refer it to this understanding: that until true peace comes, and the sabbath rest, and the number of seven decades, that is, the seventieth year, is fulfilled, neither does Jerusalem, which is interpreted vision of peace and is the Church, receive full liberty, nor do the cities of Judah, the souls that confess the Lord.

1:13.t: And the Lord answered the angel who was speaking in the prophet good words, words of consolation: good concerning the promise of things to come, consoling concerning the need of things present. These things we have given according to the letter, lest we should seem to hide from our own people what we have learned from teachers of a foreign tongue.

In short, the Lord answered good words and words of consolation, which now we see in part and prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, may the things that are in part be done away, and, set free from the Babylon of this world, may we cry out: When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became as those consoled.

1:14.t: And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with a great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the wealthy nations; for I was angry a little, but they helped toward evil. Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem in mercies, and my house shall be built in it, says the Lord of hosts; and the plumb line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem. LXX: And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with a great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the nations that have been set on top, because I indeed was angry a little, but they have set themselves on top unto evils. Therefore thus says the Lord: I will turn to Jerusalem in mercy, and my house shall be restored in it, says the Lord Almighty; and the measure shall be stretched out over Jerusalem. […]

Jerusalem and Zion, the vision of peace and the watchtower, which looks not on the wars of this world, nor on things lowly and earthly, but on peace and concord and the heights of heaven, can be understood as the Church. Angry with her because of vices and sins and charity growing colder every day, the Lord will hand her over to persecutions, so that, as in a smelting furnace, pure gold and silver may appear. But the adversaries to whom she has been handed over, striving to blot her out, fill Jerusalem with the blood of the slain from gate to gate.

1:15.t: He, then, who was jealous for Jerusalem and Zion, which are, moreover, one and the same city, is now angry with the wealthy nations, which he named above as the red, white and speckled horses: because he himself handed them over to be chastened, but they raged against those handed over; he wished them corrected as a son by a tutor, they tried to kill and punish them as an enemy. Like this is that passage in Isaiah: I gave them into your hands, but you showed them no mercy. On the old man you made the yoke very heavy, and you said: I shall be mistress forever. Now jealousy is taken ἀνθρωποπάθως (in human fashion), in the same way as anger. By this passage the heretics who disparage the Old Testament are refuted, since God, when he is angry, desires not to destroy those with whom he is angry, but to amend them.

1:16.t: Because, therefore, he says, I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with a great jealousy, which the adversaries have pressed down more than I wished, therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem not in one mercy but in many mercies, and my house, that is, the temple, shall be built in it under Zerubbabel and Joshua son of Jehozadak; and the plumb line of the masons shall be stretched out over Jerusalem.

Hence the Lord, promising peace and mercy, says that he will build her again, and that the plumb line, or the cord, is to be stretched out in her according to the measures and ranks of each one. What the cord is, is shown in the following passage, where the prophet says: I lifted up my eyes and saw: and behold, a man, and in his hand a measurers' cord. And the temple of the Lord which the adversaries destroyed can also be understood as the venerable body of the Lord, of which he himself said: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Destroyed in the passion, it was raised in the resurrection, and it was the seedbed and the beginning of all temples, of which the Apostle too speaks: You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.

1:17.t: Cry out yet, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet my cities shall overflow with good things; and the Lord shall yet comfort Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem. LXX: And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out yet, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Yet the cities shall be poured out in good things, and the Lord shall yet have mercy on Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem. The angel who had said to the prophet above: Cry out; thus says the Lord of hosts, now too urges him to cry out, not with the straining of the voice but of the mind; and this is what he commands him to cry out: Yet my cities shall overflow with good things; those which you now see laid waste by the Babylonian fire shall again abound in all things, and with present good things the Lord shall console their past misery, and shall choose Jerusalem, which a little before he had cast off. […]

1:18.t: And I lifted up my eyes and saw. And behold, four horns; and I said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these? And he said to me: These are the horns that have winnowed Judah, and Israel and Jerusalem. And the Lord showed me four smiths, and I said: What are these coming to do? He spoke, saying: These are the horns that have winnowed Judah man by man, and none of them lifted up his head, and these came to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations which have lifted up the horn over the land of Judah, to scatter it. LXX: And I lifted up my eyes and saw. And behold, four horns, and I said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these, Lord? And he said to me: These are the horns that have scattered Judah, and Israel, and Jerusalem. And the Lord showed me four smiths, and I said: What are these coming to do? And he said: These are the horns that have scattered Judah, and have broken Israel, and none of them lifted up his head, and these have gone out to sharpen them in their hands. […]

But that the prophet says he lifted up his eyes is to be fitted to the spiritual sense: I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help shall come, and: Lift up your eyes, and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest, and what we read in Isaiah: The Holy One said: Lift up your eyes, and see who has shown all these things. There is need, therefore, of the lifting up of the eyes and of spiritual understanding, that we may see the opposing powers which have lifted up their horn against us, and of which the Apostle speaks: Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of this world, of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. These four adversaries, who were always fighting against the saints, Christ crushed at his coming. And of these the psalmist says over again: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon. […]

1:20.t: These horns winnowed and scattered Judah almost man by man, so that none of them, pressed down by the heavy weight of evils, lifted up his head. The four smiths too, or craftsmen, whom the Greeks call τέκτονας, the prophet does not behold by himself, but the Lord shows them to him, and explains who the smiths and craftsmen are, whom we understand as angels obedient to the Lord's power, so that what the nations had destroyed, these may build. Now this, for which we translated from the Hebrew: These came to terrify them, namely the kingdoms, the Seventy translated: These came to sharpen them, in their hands. But sharpening them is to be taken for terrifying them. Or else they terrify, so that all may submit their necks under the yoke of Christ, and not, as someone has interpreted: when they have been sharpened, let them become worse. For if the angels come for this, to make the wicked worse, they are not to be called smiths, that is, destroyers of evils and builders of good things; […]

Against these, four smiths and, so to speak, physicians and good craftsmen are not seen by the prophet, for he could not yet see them by himself without God's showing them, but they are shown to him by the Lord: namely the four virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, of which Tully disputes most fully in the books On Duties, writing also a book of its own on the four virtues. Those, then, who destroy vices and build virtues, and all the saints who, possessing these remedies, are ever restoring the Church, are to be called smiths. Hence the Apostle too said: As a wise architect I have laid the foundation. And the Lord in his anger says that he will take away from Jerusalem the architect and the wise man. And the Lord himself, the Son of God Almighty and of the Creator of all things, is called the son of a smith. […]

2:1.t: And I lifted up my eyes, and saw; and behold, a man, and in his hand a measurers' cord. And I said: Where are you going? And he said to me: To measure Jerusalem, and to see how great is its breadth, and how great its length. LXX: And I lifted up my eyes, and saw; and behold, a man, and in his hand a geometer's cord. And I said to him: Where are you going? And he said to me: To measure out Jerusalem, and to see how great is its breadth, and how great its length. He who before, with eyes lifted up, had seen sad things in the four horns, now again lifts up his eyes to see the man of whom it is written: Behold a man, the Rising is his name, of whom we also read above: And behold a man mounting upon a red horse, and he was standing among the myrtles that were in the deep, or, among the shady mountains. And of whom the Father speaks: He has built my city, whose craftsman and founder is God. […]

2:3.t: And behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him: Run, speak to this boy, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall, because of the multitude of men and cattle in its midst. And I will be to it, says the Lord, a wall of fire round about, and I will be in glory in its midst. LXX: And behold, the angel who spoke in me was standing, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him, saying: Run and speak to that youth, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited fruitful from the multitude of men and cattle in its midst. And I will be to it, says the Lord, a wall of fire round about, and I will be for glory in its midst. The angel who spoke in the prophet, and was standing, or, as is read in the Hebrew, was going out, for that is what iasa means, the Hebrews think to be Michael. […]

But because in certain passages of Scripture we have learned that some things are done through the cherubim, and other things through the seraphim, whether they do these things by themselves, or whether they are done through the hosts subject to them, which, as is said, receive the names of the greater ones because they come from the greater ones, we do not wish to affirm what we do not prove by clear testimonies. This, however, we know most certainly, that to carry out service from above, some spirits send others, as the prophet Zechariah testifies, who says: Behold, the angel who was speaking in me went forth; and behold, another angel went forth to meet him, and he said to him: Run, and speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls. For when an angel says to an angel "Run and speak," there is no doubt that one sends another. Those who are sent are lesser, those who send are greater.

2:4.t: And Jerusalem, he says, shall be inhabited without a wall because of the multitude of men and cattle, or, with an abundance of all fruits. Some interpret men and cattle as two peoples, of the Jews and of the Gentiles: that those who were versed in the law and came to the faith of Christ are called men, while we, who after idolatry were as it were in the desert of the law and the solitude of the prophets, and have received his passion, ought to be called cattle. But others want all rational men, learned in the knowledge of the Scriptures, to be understood as men, and as cattle all the simple among the believers, and that of these it is said: Men and cattle you will save, O Lord.

But we, according to the spiritual sense, interpret all these things of the Church, which is inhabited without a wall, or, as the Seventy translated, κατάκαρπος, that is, with an abundance of all fruits, and has a multitude of men and cattle, and the Lord is fire round about her, and he himself dwells in glory in her midst. This is the city of which we read elsewhere: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God, and again: Great is the Lord and exceedingly to be praised, in the city of our God, in his holy mountain. Whoever dwells in her can say: But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, and: The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture, there he has set me. By the water of refreshment he has brought me up.

All these things the Jews think will come carnally under the ἠλειμμένῳ (anointed one), whom they promise themselves with the vainest hope: that Jerusalem will have such great blessedness that, because of the multitude of men and of all cattle, it cannot have a wall; but the defense of the Lord himself will be its wall, and it will enjoy the glory of him who dwells in its midst.

2:5.t: These cattle and these living creatures hear the voice of the good shepherd, and know it, and follow him, because he is both the shepherd, who also rules us, and the door, because through him we enter into the Church and to the Father, and a wall of fire round about, so that he may warm those who believe and dwell in the midst, who before had grown lukewarm from the coldness of charity, and that they may be fervent in spirit. But the wolves and the most savage beasts — of which it is written: Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you, and whose fruit is hay, wood, stubble, and they bring forth thistles and thorns —, let him consume with his fire; and he who is fire to the adversaries, let him be glory in the midst of the believers. That the Lord is the wall of Jerusalem we read in another place too: Mountains round about it, and the Lord round about his people.

2:6.t: O, O, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord; for I have scattered you into the four winds of heaven, says the Lord. O Zion, arise, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts: After glory he has sent me to the nations that despoiled you; for he who touches you touches the pupil of his eye. For behold, I lift up my hand over them, and they shall be spoil for those who served them, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me. LXX: O, O, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for from the four winds of heaven I will gather you, says the Lord. In Zion be saved, you who inhabit the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the Lord Almighty: After glory he has sent me to the nations that despoiled you, for he who touches you, as it were touches the pupil of his eye. Behold, I will bring my hand upon them, and they shall be spoil for those who had served them, and you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me. […]

2:8.t: "Say no evil thing, my brothers, against Him that was crucified, and treat not scornfully the stripes wherewith all may be healed, even as we are healed. For it will be well if, persuaded by the Scriptures, you are circumcised from hard-heartedness: not that circumcision which you have from the tenets that are put into you; for that was given for a sign, and not for a work of righteousness, as the Scriptures compel you [to admit]. Assent, therefore, and pour no ridicule on the Son of God; obey not the Pharisaic teachers, and scoff not at the King of Israel, as the rulers of your synagogues teach you to do after your prayers: for if he that touches those who are not pleasing to God, is as one that touches the apple of God's eye, how much more so is he that touches His beloved! And that this is He, has been sufficiently demonstrated."

[Passage quoted, Zech. ii. 8.]

IF, then, the Lord that sent (Him) is Lord Almighty, and He that says He was sent is so also, surely there are Two; And He that was sent as Almighty Lord of the nations says clearly, "He sent me."
2:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 25

2:8.t:
[Passage quoted, Zech. ii. 8.]

IN these words the Almighty Lord Himself says that He has been sent, and teaches who it was that sent Him, saying, "And ye shall know that the Almighty Lord has sent me." Here, then, you have clearly two Persons using one Name, the Almighty Lord that sent, and Him that is sent having the same Name as the Sender. And whom else could you suppose Him that is sent to be, but Him that we have so often called God the Word, Who states that He is sent by the Father, and says clearly, "After his glory he has sent me," shewing that though pre-existing in the glory of the Father He was sent afterwards unto the nations that spoiled you? For the Word of God was sent unto the nations, who before were hostile to the people of God, and subjected them to Himself, making a spoil of them by His disciples, who belonged to the Jewish nation, which the Gentiles had long spoiled enslaving it to their own idolatry. This, then, He says that the nations will suffer, as He ordained. […]
2:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 16

2:8.t: But what follows: Thus says the Lord of hosts, after glory he has sent me, and the rest, introduces the voice of the Savior speaking, who, being almighty God, says that he was sent by the almighty Father, not according to that by which he is almighty, but according to that by which he was sent after glory. Who, though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, the death of the cross. Nor is it a wonder that Christ is called almighty, in whose person we read in the Apocalypse of John: Thus says the faithful witness, the beginning of the creation of God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Lord God Almighty. That too which we read in Psalm 23 (24): Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the king of glory shall enter, and which again is said by other angels who did not know the mystery of the flesh assumed: Who is this king of glory? […]

But as for what he says: He who touches you touches the pupil of his eye, take the touching as harassment and injury, according to what we read: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets. For whoever touches the saints of the Lord is as one who desires to harm the pupil of his eye, and strives to deprive him of the clear light, of which he speaks in the Gospel: You are the light of the world.

He was sent, therefore, after the glory of the divine majesty, to the nations that despoiled the people of God, so that those who had formerly plundered them might be spoil for those who served them, and the whole crowd of those who once served might know that the Lord Almighty has sent him.

Another example to prove the same point may be found in a passage of Zechariah where the "Almighty" sends the "Almighty." This can only mean that God the Father sends God the Son. The text runs, "So says the Lord Almighty: 'After the glory he has sent me to the nations that have robbed you; for he that touches you touches the apple of my eye. For behold, I lift up my head upon them, and they shall be a prey to those who served them; and you shall know that the Lord almighty sent me.' " In this case, the Lord almighty says that he is sent by the Lord almighty. How can anyone doubt that it is Christ who is speaking and, in fact, speaking to the lost sheep of the house of Israel? Remember what is said in the Gospel: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." The comparison of these lost sheep to the apple of God's eye is explained by the perfection of God's love. And, of course, it was to this flock of sheep that the apostles belonged. […]

Suppose for the sake of the argument that what we said was true only of all the most powerful and noble. Were the vices that were common to noble and ignoble alike less serious? I mean the hatred and abuse of all holy men, for surely it is a sort of sacrilege to hate those who worship God. Just as the man who injures our slaves thereby harms us, and the man who flogs another's sons tortures the father's affection by his children's suffering, so anyone who injures a servant of God violates the divine majesty, as the Lord said to his apostle: "He that receiveth you, receiveth me, and he that despiseth you, despiseth me.'' Our most gracious and loving Lord shared his honor and disgrace alike with his servants, to the end that no one who injured a servant of God should think that the man alone was hurt by his action, since injury to God would undoubtedly be mingled with the harm inflicted on his followers. […]
2:8.s: On the Government of God, Book 8, Chapter 3

2:9.t: And God lifts up his hand to strike the hostile nations, and to lead his people back either into Jerusalem or into the Church. By the hostile nations, according to tropology, understand the opposing powers, which every day subject sinners to their power and compel them to serve them.

2:10.t:
And if it be admitted to be a noble privilege to be and to be reckoned the people of God, and if this one thing is the noblest of the divine promises, that God should say of those who are worthy of Him, "I will be their God, and they shall be my people," Israel was naturally proud in days of old of being the only people of God, but now the Lord has come to sojourn with us and promises graciously to extend this privilege to the Gentiles, saying:

"Lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, and many nations shall flee unto the Lord, and they shall be to him a people."

On which I may aptly quote : "And I will say to a people that were not my people, Ye are my people. And they shall say, Thou art the Lord our God."
2:10.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

2:10.t:
[Passage quoted, Zech. ii. 10, 11.]

AND this prophecy is like the former one, telling of the coming of the Christ to men, and the call of the Gentiles to salvation through Him.

"For I the Lord myself will come," He says, "and at My coming no longer Israel of old, nor one single nation of the earth alone, but many nations shall take refuge in the greater and high Lord, the God of Me Myself and of the Universe, to Whom fleeing the nations shall reap the great harvest of being called and actually becoming the people of God, and of dwelling in the midst of her that is called the daughter of Zion."

So it is common in Holy Scripture to call the Church of God on earth, as being as it were a daughter of the heavenly Zion. And this good news is told in the oracle which says:

"Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Zion, because I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee." For we believe that God the Word dwells in the midst of the Church. […]
2:10.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 26

2:10.t:
[Passage quoted, Zech. ii. 10.]

As it is now my object to unfold from the prophets the second cause of our Lord's living our life on earth, the prophecy before us appears to state it so clearly that it hardly needs any elaboration. You will notice that He gives the cause of His coming, where He says, "And many nations shall flee unto the Lord in that day, and they shall be to me for a people." And the Word announces this to the daughter of Sion, calling the Church of God by this name, through her seeming to be the daughter of the heavenly Jerusalem, she that is the mother of the Saints, according to the holy apostle. […]

2:10.t: So prophesied Zechariah after the Return from Babylon, in the reign of Darius, King of Persia, when Jerusalem was but just arisen from the desolation which it suffered under the Babylonians. And the whole period from Darius the Persian, in whose time Zechariah prophesied, even to Augustus, Emperor of Rome, amounts to the seven and sixty-two weeks of years in Daniel, which are equivalent to 483 years, as I have shewn in my recent investigations. And neither in the time of the Macedonians from Alexander onwards, not even if you include the reign of Augustus, was anything similar to the words of the prophet fulfilled. For when in those days did the Lord, Whom the prophet speaks of as divine, come among men, and many nations know Him, and confess Him to the only God, and take refuge in Him, and be to Him a people?
2:10.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 4

2:10.t: The Lord heard the prayer of the prophets. The Father did not despise our race, which was perishing; he sent from heaven his own Son the Lord as our physician. One of the prophets says, "The Lord whom you seek, comes; and he shall come suddenly." Where will he come? "The Lord shall come to his temple," where you took up stones against him. Another of the prophets, on hearing this, says to him, "In speaking of God's salvation, do you speak softly? In announcing the good tidings of God's coming for salvation, do you speak in secret?" "Go up onto a high mountain, Zion, herald of glad tidings; say to the cities of Judah"—what shall I say?—"Here is your God! Here comes with power the Lord God." Again the Lord himself has said, " 'Behold, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you,' says the Lord. 'And many nations shall be joined to the Lord.' " The Israelites rejected salvation through me; "I come to gather nations of every language," for, "he came unto his own, and his own received him not." […]

But rightly, after the captivity, is the daughter of Zion called forth to joy, of whom it is also said in the psalm: When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult, and Israel shall be glad.

But who this people is that is comforted through the Apostles and churchmen, not Israel and Jacob and Judah, as Scripture records in other places, but the people of God, the prophet Zechariah testifies, saying: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion: for I will come and dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord. And many nations shall flee to the Lord in that day, and shall be his people, and they shall dwell in the midst of you, and they shall know that the Lord almighty has sent me to you (Zech 2:10, 11). By this testimony it is clearly shown that very many nations are to be turned into the people of God. And these things the Lord says, sent by the Lord whose name is Almighty.

Praise and rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord. And many nations shall be joined to the Lord on that day, and they shall be my people, and I will dwell in the midst of you, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. And the Lord shall possess Judah as his portion in the sanctified land, and he shall yet choose Jerusalem. LXX: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I will come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord. And many nations shall flee for refuge to the Lord on that day, and they shall be his people, and they shall dwell in the midst of you, and you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you, and the Lord shall possess Judah as his portion in the holy land, and he shall yet choose Jerusalem. […]

2:11.t: Some of the Jews think that these things were in part fulfilled under Zerubbabel and Joshua, Ezra and Nehemiah, especially since Jerusalem is chosen and Judah is possessed; that is to say, the two tribes which returned from the Babylonian captivity and were called Judah, and not Israel, which lives among the Medes to this day. Others, however, defer them to the future: that then the nations are to believe in him who is sent by the Lord, and Jerusalem is to be chosen; although surely all the nations have already believed in the Lord Savior, and a city that has been utterly destroyed cannot be chosen.

2:13.t: Let all flesh be silent before the face of the Lord, for he has risen up from his holy dwelling. LXX: Let all flesh fear before the face of the Lord, for he has risen from his holy clouds. Since these things are so, and the Lord is going to possess Judah as his portion and to choose Jerusalem, let the whole race of men dread the coming of the Lord, for he has risen up from his holy dwelling. Now the Lord is said to rise, and as it were to awaken from sleep, when he rises up to avenge his people, according to what is written: Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord? Or else, according to the LXX, who said: He has risen from his holy clouds, understand the patriarchs, prophets and apostles, whom the Lord commanded not to rain rain upon Israel. These are the clouds of which it is written: And let the clouds sprinkle justice; for these bodily clouds, into which the denser air is gathered, cannot rain justice. In these clouds and with these clouds the Lord says in the Gospel that he will come. […]

3:1.t: Also in Zechariah: "And the Lord showed me Jesus, that great priest, standing before the face of the angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand to oppose him. And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments, and he stood before the face of the angel himself; and he answered them and said to them who were standing before his face, saying, 'Take away his filthy garments from him.' And he said to him, 'Behold, I have taken away your iniquities.' And put upon him a priestly garment, and set a fair miter upon his head." Also Paul to the Philippians: "Who being established in the form of God, thought it not robbery that he was equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, even the death of the cross. 3:1.t:
[Passages quoted, Zech. iii. 1—6, 9; vi. 9-13.]

In this passage too the prophet-high-priest called Jesus presents, I think, a very clear picture and plain symbol of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, being honoured by bearing His Name, and made the leader of the return of the people from the Babylonian captivity. Since, also, our Saviour Jesus Christ is said by the Prophet Isaiah to have been sent to preach liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to comfort all that mourn, and to give to all that mourn in Zion glory for dust, the ointment of gladness. You have, therefore, her two great High Priests, first the Christ in Moses, and second the Jesus of whom I am speaking, both bearing in themselves the signs of the truth concerning our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. 3:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 17

3:1.t: Whenever I remember Zechariah, I shudder at the reaping-hook, and likewise at his testimony against the priests, his hints in reference to the celebrated Joshua, the high priest, whom he represents as stripped of filthy and unbecoming garments and then clothed in rich priestly apparel. As for the words and charges to Joshua which he puts into the angel's mouth, let them be treated with silent respect, as referring perhaps to a greater and higher object than those who are many priests: but even at his right hand stood the devil, to resist him. A fact, in my eyes, of no slight significance, and demanding no slight fear and watchfulness.

For in that passage too, in giving the name of High Priest to Him Who made with His own Blood the priestly propitiation for our sins, he does not by the word "made" declare the first existence of the Only-begotten, but says "made" with the intention of representing that grace which is commonly spoken of in connection with the appointment of priests. For Jesus, the great High Priest (as Zechariah says), Who offered up his own lamb, that is, His own Body, for the sin of the world; Who, by reason of the children that are partakers of flesh and blood, Himself also in like manner took part with them in blood (not in that He was in the beginning, being the Word and God, and being in the form of God, and equal with God, but in that He emptied Himself in the form of the servant, and offered an oblation and sacrifice for us), He, I say, became a High Priest many generations later, after the order of Melchisedech. […]

But because he forgot the commandment of God and fulfilled the will of the serpent, the devil held his hand and caused him to reach for the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, in order to eat of the forbidden fruit. In him, judgment was pronounced on all, and the adversary began to stand at the right hand of all. Hence, that cursed form came forth against Judas: And let the Devil stand at his right hand (Psalm 108:6). If that curse is severe, then this blessing is the greatest, by which the chains of harsh curses are loosened. Therefore, the Lord Jesus placed the devil at His right hand, just as we read in the book of Zechariah (Zach. III, 1); for He had taken up the cause and place of mankind.
3:1.s: THE PRAYER OF JOB AND DAVID 3:10.27

3:1.t: And he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord. And Satan was standing at his right hand, to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan: The Lord rebuke you, Satan, and the Lord rebuke you, he who has chosen Jerusalem. Is not this a brand plucked out of the fire? And Joshua was clothed in filthy garments, and was standing before the face of the angel, who answered and said to those who were standing before him, saying: Take away the filthy garments from him. And he said to him: Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you, and I have clothed you with changes of raiment. And he said: Put a clean tiara upon his head; and they put a clean tiara upon his head, and they clothed him with garments. LXX: And the Lord showed me Joshua the high priest, standing before the face of the angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand, to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: The Lord rebuke you, devil, and the Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you. […]

Our writers, however, explain it thus: that he is the high priest to whom it is said: You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek. Since he cannot be seen of himself, he is shown to the prophet by the Lord, standing before the angel of the Lord, whom they take to be the angel of great counsel: not that he is one and another, so that we should admit two persons in the Son, but that he is one and the same, and is both shown as a man in soiled clothing and said to appear as an angel, the mediator of men and God. And that he is not Joshua son of Jehozadak they try to show from this, that the words son of Jehozadak are not added in the present place, whereas in other places, where it is truly Joshua son of Jehozadak who is spoken of, he is always registered by his father's name. So Jesus is seen standing, set firm with a steady step: And Satan standing at his right hand, to oppose him. For he was tempted in every way, without sin. […]

But to sinners the devil stands at the right hand. Yet that discussion is another matter. Whoever is a sinner, the devil stands at his right hand. But someone says: How is it that in Zechariah it is said to stand also to Jesus the son of Josedech? "And the devil was standing at his right hand." How is it written in Zechariah that the devil stands at the right hand of the Savior? You see that there is a question here. But at that time when the devil was standing at the right hand of the Savior, "Jesus," it says, "had filthy garments." He was bearing our sins, he was wrapped in our vices: therefore the devil was standing at his right hand.

It is written in Zechariah: "And he showed me Jesus the great priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand, to fight with him." If, then, the devil stands at the right hand of the Lord, how does he now say of Judas, And let the devil stand at his right hand? But see what he says. The devil stood at the right hand of Jesus to oppose him: that is, he wished to be an adversary to his right hand. But here he does not say that he wishes to fight, but that he had already conquered Judas. There the devil desires to fight against the right hand; but here he has gained mastery over the right hand of Judas. But this too must be considered. At that time he stood at the Lord's right hand to oppose him, when Jesus had filthy garments. For so it is written there as well: "And Jesus had filthy garments." As long as the Lord Jesus has filthy garments, so long does the devil stand at his right hand: as long as he bears our sins, in our sins the devil opposes him. […]

But perhaps an inquisitive reader will object this too: how we can assert that God stands at the right of the just man, and the devil at the left of the sinner, when concerning our Lord it is read in Zechariah, "And the devil was standing at his right hand to oppose him." Let him, then, who objects this read also what follows: that when the devil was standing at his right hand, Jesus had filthy garments. Rightly did he who had taken up our sins and was bearing our offenses have the devil at his right hand, not so much for himself as for the filthy garments. And at the same time let him consider that it is not said, "The devil was standing as victor and triumphing," but as still set in the contest and in the battle-line and in doubt—indeed, when he had not yet begun to fight. For it follows, "That he might oppose him." But the devil was opposing him, as we said, because he had filthy garments from our sins. […]

3:2.t:
[Passage quoted, Zech. iii. 1.]

AND here again the Lord says that another Lord will rebuke the devil. The Lord that is speaking with Him is not himself the rebuker, but tells of another Lord. Wherein I consider there is clear proof of the existence of two Lords, the Father and God of the Universe, and One after the Father, Who has received the lordship and dominion of all things begotten.
3:2.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 27

3:2.t: You can search them out for yourself from sacred Scripture without my help. And it will become clearly evident to you that this likely is the age of which it was said, "Believe not in friends and trust not in princes," and that the prophecy is now being fulfilled: "The leaders of my people have not known me; they are foolish and senseless children. They are wise to do evils, but to do good they have no knowledge." We should rather pity such people than hate them and should rather pray for them than revile them. For we were created to bless and not to revile. Thus also Michael, when he was arguing with the devil over the body of Moses, did not dare to bring an accusation of blasphemy against him even for such a serious offense but said, "May the Lord rebuke you." Even in Zechariah, we read something similar to this. "The Lord rebuke you, O Satan, and the Lord that chose Jerusalem rebuke you." And so we also pray that those who refuse to be rebuked by their friends with humility may be rebuked by the Lord.
3:2.s: Against Rufinus 2.18 (as quoted by Jerome, AD 420)

3:2.t: And the Lord said to Satan, to the accuser and his adversary, for he is the enemy and avenger, the accuser of his brothers: The Lord rebuke you, Satan, as the Lord rained from the Lord, and the Lord rebuke you, he who has chosen Jerusalem. Since, then, out of all the cities of Judah Jerusalem has now been chosen, the Lord in no way imputing to her the sins she committed, why do you try to overwhelm Joshua like a brand, which is commonly called a firebrand, Joshua who escaped as it were half-burnt from the Babylonian captivity?

As for what follows: The Lord rebuke you, Satan, and the Lord rebuke you, he who has chosen Jerusalem, they explain it thus: that the Father and the Son is Lord, and in Psalm 109 (110) we read: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand; he speaks of the other Lord, not because the Lord himself who speaks cannot rebuke, but because, from the unity of their nature, when the other has rebuked, he himself who speaks rebukes: For he who sees the Son sees the Father, and he it is who has chosen Jerusalem, the Church, which contemplates the peace of the Lord. Now the brand plucked out of the fire can most rightly be understood as him who, though he was in Babylon, was not consumed by the Babylonian fire, nor touched by the flame of this world. Hence Moses too, in the wilderness, sees a great vision, in which the bush was burning and was not consumed.

3:3.t: "But to give you the account of the revelation of the holy Jesus Christ, I take up again my discourse, and I assert that even that revelation was made for us who believe on Christ the High Priest, namely this crucified One; and though we lived in fornication and all kinds of filthy conversation, we have by the grace of our Jesus, according to His Father's will, stripped ourselves of all those filthy wickednesses with which we were imbued. And though the devil is ever at hand to resist us, and anxious to seduce all to himself, yet the Angel of God, i.e., the Power of God sent to us through Jesus Christ, rebukes him, and he departs from us. And we are just as if drawn out from the fire, when purified from our former sins, and [rescued] from the affliction and the fiery trial by which the devil and all his coadjutors try us; out of which Jesus the Son of God has promised again to deliver us, and invest us with prepared garments, if we do His commandments; and has undertaken to provide an eternal kingdom [for us]. […]

Every soul that has been clothed with a human body has its own "filth". And that you may know that Jesus too was made filthy by his own will, because for our salvation he had assumed a human body, listen to the prophet Zechariah saying: "Jesus was clothed with filthy garments". And this indeed makes against those who deny that our Lord had a human body, but say it was woven of heavenly and spiritual things. For if his body was of heavenly things and, as they falsely assert, of the stars and some other more sublime and spiritual nature, let them answer why a spiritual body could be filthy, or how they interpret what we have set down: "Jesus was clothed with filthy garments". […]
3:3.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

3:3.t: Now in this, by that wondrous sacrifice, Elijah clearly proclaimed to us the sacramental rite of baptism that should afterwards be instituted. For the fire was kindled by water thrice poured upon it, so that it is clearly shown that where the mystic water is, there is the kindling, warm and fiery spirit that burns up the ungodly and illuminates the faithful. Yes, and yet again his disciple Elisha, when Naaman the Syrian, who was diseased with leprosy, had come to him as a suppliant, cleanses the sick man by washing him in the Jordan, clearly indicating what should come, both by the use of water generally and by dipping in the river in particular. For the Jordan alone of rivers, receiving in itself the firstfruits of sanctification and benediction, conveyed in its channel to the whole world, as it were from some fount in the type afforded by itself, the grace of baptism. These then are indications in deed and act of regeneration in baptism. Let us for the rest consider the prophecies of it in words and language. […]

As for what follows: Joshua was clothed in filthy garments, they interpret it in three ways: either on account of the unlawful marriage, or on account of the sins of the people, or because of the squalor of the captivity. Now the angel before whose face Joshua was standing commanded the other angels, in the person of the Lord, to take away from him the filthy garments of which we spoke above. When they had fulfilled the command in deed, the same angel speaks again to Joshua: Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you; these are the filthy garments; and I have clothed you with changes of raiment; that is, I have joined an Israelite wife to you; for which the Seventy translated ποδήρη, which we can call an ankle-length tunic, because it flows down to the ankles and feet.

This Jesus was clothed in filthy garments, who, though he had committed no sin, was made sin for us. And he bears our infirmities, and grieves for us, and we reckoned him to be in sorrow, and under a blow, and in anguish. But he was wounded for our iniquities, and was made weak for our sins. And in the apostle Paul we read: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. It is he who speaks in Psalm 21 (22): Far from my salvation are the words of my offences. And in Psalm 68 (69): O God, you know my foolishness, and my offences are not hidden from you. All these are called filthy garments, and they will be taken away from him when he has blotted out our sins, so that, because he was clothed in filthy garments, we, rising again, may hear in him after baptism: Let your garments be always white; and the whole Church of believers hears through Isaiah: Wash yourselves, be clean. And of her it is prophesied in the Song of Songs: Who is this who comes up made white? […]

Holy Job says, when speaking about his own sins, "for man that is born of a woman is short-lived and full of wrath: as the flower of grass, so does he fall; and he departs like a shadow, nor shall he stay. Hast Thou not taken account even of him, and caused him to enter into judgment in Thy sight? For who shall be pure from uncleanness? Not even one, even if his life should be but of one day upon the earth." Now when he speaks of uncleanness here, the mere perusal of the passage is enough to show that he meant sin to be understood. It is plain from the words, of what he is speaking. The same phrase and sense occur in the prophet Zechariah, in the place where "the filthy garments" are removed from off the high priest, and it is said to him, "I have taken away thy sins." Well now, I rather think that all these passages, and others of like import, which point to the fact that man is born in sin and under the curse, are not to be read among the dark recesses of the Manicheans, but in the sunshine of catholic truth.

3:5.t: And as for what follows: Put a clean tiara upon his head, for tiara we read in the Hebrew Saniph, which most people call a mitre; and by this they want the dignity of the priesthood to be understood, because, once the filth of his sins had been taken away, he held a clean priesthood. This is what the Jews say.

3:6.t:
And the angel of the Lord was standing.

And the angel of the Lord solemnly charged Joshua, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: If you walk in my ways and keep my charge, you also shall judge my house, and shall keep my courts, and I will give you those who walk, from among these who now stand by here. LXX: And the angel of the Lord was standing. And the angel of the Lord solemnly charged Joshua, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: If you walk in my ways and keep my precepts, you too shall judge my house; and if you keep my court, I will give you those who shall move about in the midst of these who stand here. The Hebrews, following the course of the interpretation they have begun, understand these things to have been said by the angel of the Lord to Joshua (Iesus, the same name as Jesus) son of Jehozadak: that after the removal of the filthy garments and the restoration of the dignity of a clean priesthood, he is given a command according to what is written in the Gospel: Behold, you have been made well; […]

3:8.t: Of Him He has also spoken by the mouth of the prophet Ezekiel, saying, "I will set up one Shepherd over them, and He shall feed them, even My Servant David, He shall feed them, and He shall be their Shepherd. And I the Lord will be their God, and My Servant David a Prince among them." Now king David was already dead, and therefore the true David, the truly humble, the truly meek, the true Son of God, strong of hand, is announced by this name; he also is intended in the book of the prophet Zechariah, where God the Father says, "Behold I will send my servant, the Orient is His name." Did then His being "clothed in filthy garments" deprive the Sun of righteousness of the brightness of His Godhead?

Those who want the high priest and his friends to be understood as the Lord Savior and his disciples take the men τερατοσκόπους, men who portend, in this way: they refer them to the apostles, who perceived his mystical signs and recognized the future from the present; while in the man who was blind from birth they interpret the restored eyes as concerning the people of the Gentiles, and in the woman with the flow of blood they explain the Church as set free from the works of blood.

Hear, O Joshua, high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are men who portend. For behold, I will bring my servant the Rising, for behold the stone which I have given before Joshua: upon one stone are seven eyes. LXX: Hear then, O Joshua, high priest, and your neighbours who sit before your face, for the men τερατοσκόποι, that is, of portents, are beholders, for behold, I will bring my servant the Rising, for the stone which I have given before the face of Joshua, upon one stone are seven eyes. Our writers are hard pressed in this place by the Jews, on the ground that, following the sequence and texture of the discourse, they ought rather to understand Joshua (Iesus, the same name as Jesus) the priest, son of Jehozadak, than the Lord Savior. […]

3:9.t: As for what follows: For behold the stone which I have given before Joshua, the lovers of the history understand it of Christ in this way, saying that Christ was to come after Joshua son of Jehozadak. For this, they say, is what before Joshua means, that is, in his sight and before his face, so that it signifies things to come; and he is called a stone for his strength and hardness, with which he crushed all kingdoms, the stone which we also read in Daniel was cut from the mountain without hands.

Behold, I will engrave its carving, says the Lord of hosts, and I will take away the iniquity of that land in one day.

On that day, says the Lord of hosts, a man shall call his friend under the vineyard and under the fig tree. LXX: Behold, I will dig a pit, says the Lord Almighty, and I will handle all the iniquity of that land in one day. On that day, says the Lord Almighty, each one shall call his neighbour under the vine and under the fig tree. Above he had said: Behold the stone which I have given before Joshua, upon one stone are seven eyes. Now, consistently, he keeps the μεταφορὰν (metaphor) taken from the stone, and says: I will engrave its carving, or I will carve its engraving. For where it is written in Hebrew maphate phethee, Aquila translated διαγλύψω ἄνοιγμα αὐτῆς, that is, I will carve its opening; Theodotion and Symmachus, I will carve its carving. […]

As for what is written according to the Seventy: Behold, I will dig a pit, we can understand the ditch or pit in place of the carving of the stone: for everything that is carved is also dug. Yet if someone, more contentiously, will not refer this to the stone, but would have it hold, as it were, its own beginning and its own meaning, let us say that the Lord Almighty, on the day of his Son's passion, or else — as the Jews think, at the final end of the world, when he comes to judge — digs out and brings into the open the works of each person, and handles the whole earth on the day of judgment; for this is the one day, and on that day each of the saints calls his companions and friends, who are themselves also saints, to rest, and rejoices in the virtue of his works.

These are the "seven eyes" of the Lamb, and the "seven facets" of the stone mentioned by Zachary, and the seven days that followed upon the first light. These Centers are the "seven golden lamp-stands," and Christ "in the midst of the seven lamp-stands," which are the seven illuminations of wisdom, that is, the metaphysical, the natural, the mathematical, the logical, the ethical, the political, and the theological.

3:10.t: On that day of the passion of Christ, the man who is perfect in Christ, and who with the apostles ascends to the summit of the Lord's goodwill, shall call his neighbour, either the believers from among the Jews or at any rate the people of the Gentiles, under the vineyard which is called Sorek, and of which he says in the Gospel: I am the vine, and whose fruit gladdens the heart of man; and under the fig tree, the sweetest fruits of the Holy Spirit, so that they may rest in eternal peace and, the sedition of the world and the gore of warriors having been suppressed, may know that they are under a king whose name, mystically in Solomon, is that of peace. Of this same sitting under the vineyard and under the fig tree the prophet Micah also makes mention, saying: On that day each one shall call his neighbour and his brother under the fig tree and his vineyard, and there shall be none to terrify them.

4:1.t: And the angel who was speaking in me returned, and roused me like a man who is roused from his sleep. LXX: And the angel who was speaking in me returned, and roused me as a man is wont to be roused from his sleep. For where had he gone, that he should return, especially he who was speaking in the prophet, and who could not be apart from him in whom he was speaking? But whenever human frailty is left to its own weakness, we must believe that God, and the help of his angels, departs from us. So the prophet too, stunned with amazement at the great vision, was numb in his whole mind and could not see the clear light of truth; hence he is roused from the past vision to another vision, as though waking from sleep, so that he may see what with closed eyes he did not see. Let us also say it another way. There is a testimony in the Proverbs of Solomon: If you sit down, you will be without fear; […]

4:2.t: Behold the seven horns of the Lamb, the seven eyes of God -the seven eyes are the seven spirits of the Lamb; seven torches burning before the throne of God seven golden candlesticks, seven young sheep, the seven women in Isaiah, the seven churches in Paul, seven deacons, seven angels, seven trumpets, seven seals to the book, seven periods of seven days with which Pentecost is completed, the seven weeks in Daniel, also the forty-three weeks in Daniel; with Noah, seven of all clean things in the ark; seven revenges of Cain, seven years for a debt to be acquitted, the lamp with seven orifices, seven pillars of wisdom in the house of Solomon.
4:2.s: On the Creation of the World

4:2.t: Now let us discuss what has been written by churchmen in their commentaries. They understand the golden lampstand of purest gold as the Church, which in the holy Scriptures searches out the sense and the mind rather than the words. And that gold is taken to mean the sense is shown by the back and shoulders of the dove in Psalm 67 (68), which are said to shine with the green or the gleam of gold. The lamp they too understand as Christ himself, because he shines in the Church, he who said of himself: No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, that is, under the measure of the law, but upon a lampstand, that is, the freedom of the Gospel, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. The seven lamps and their pourers they too understand as the graces of the Holy Spirit, through which the Church receives the oil of the mercy of God and of all the virtues. […]

And he said to me: What do you see? And I said: I have seen, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, and its lamp upon its head; and its seven lamps upon it, seven and seven pourers for the lamps which were upon its head. And two olive trees upon it, one on the right of the lamp, and one on its left. And I answered, and I say to the angel who was speaking in me, saying: What are these, my lord? And the angel who was speaking in me answered, and said to me: Do you not know what these are? And I said: No, my lord. And he answered, and said to me, saying: This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my spirit, says the Lord of hosts. Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel? Into a plain! And he shall bring out the chief stone, and shall make equal the grace of its grace. LXX: And he said to me: What do you see? And I said: I have seen, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, and a lamp upon it; and seven lamps upon it, and seven pourers of the lamps which were upon it. […]

4:7.t: And again the Prophet Zechariah also prophesied about that stone which is Christ. For he said:—I saw a chief stone of equality and of love. And why did he say “chief”? Surely because from the beginning He was with His Father. And again that he spoke of love, it was because when He came into the world, He said thus to His disciples:—This is My commandment, that ye love one another. And again He said:—I have called you My friends (lovers). And the blessed Apostle said thus:—God loved as in the love of His Son. Of a truth Christ loved us and gave Himself for us.

And what follows: Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel? Into a plain!; they understand it as said to the devil, who stood at the right hand of Joshua to oppose him, and lifted himself up against Zerubbabel and the people of the Jews. But he has been turned into a plain and humbled, and he lies under the feet of Israel, because God shall bring out the chief stone, Christ his Son, who was always a help to the people of Israel. And his grace, that is, the grace of the stone, toward those whom he brought back from captivity, shall make equal the grace which he always exercised toward their fathers. This we have found said by the Hebrews.

But most of our writers interpret the mountain as the devil, and the Antichrist, who dares to stand before Zerubbabel, from whom Christ was to be born, and to raise himself up, and to say in the Gospel: All these things have been delivered to me, and I will give them to you, if you will fall down and worship me. And the Lord, laying him low under his feet, and making him humble instead of proud, and cast down, says: Get behind, Satan; for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve. And they give as an example in the Gospel the lunatic, whom the apostles had not been able to heal; they ask why they could not heal him, and they hear: Amen I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain: Pass from here, and it will pass; and nothing will be impossible to you. But this kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting. There the mountain is plainly taken to mean the devil. […]

4:9.t: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: The hands of Zerubbabel have founded this house, and his hands shall finish it, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. For who has despised the small days? And they shall rejoice, and shall see the stone of tin in the hand of Zerubbabel. These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which run to and fro through the whole earth. LXX: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: The hands of Zerubbabel have founded this house, and his hands shall complete it. And you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you; for who has despised in the small days? And they shall rejoice, and shall see the stone of tin in the hand of Zerubbabel; these seven are the eyes of the Lord, which look upon all the earth. Much is said both by the Hebrews and by our writers; following most of it and rejecting some, let us set out what we think, keeping the truth of the history, so that from it we may be able to recognize him who is prophesied through the history. […]

Many of our writers interpret the hands of Zerubbabel, who founded the house and himself finished it, as Christ. But if we accept this, we shall be compelled to explain who the stone of tin in the hand of Zerubbabel is. For surely another Christ is not to be shown in the hand of Christ? Although some have taken the stone of tin as the body of the Lord, which was soiled by no stains of sins, and is not called lead, but purest tin.

4:10.t: Wherefore to those seven days the Lord attributed to each a thousand years; for thus went the warning: "In Thine eyes, O Lord, a thousand years are as one day." Therefore in the eyes of the Lord each thousand of years is ordained, for I find that the Lord's eyes are seven. Wherefore, as I have narrated, that true Sabbath will be in the seventh millenary of years, when Christ with His elect shall reign.
4:10.s: On the Creation of the World

4:10.t: And definitely did He show concerning this stone:—Lo! on this stone will I open seven eyes. And what then are the seven eyes that were opened on the stone? Clearly the Spirit of God that abode on Christ with seven operations, as Isaiah the Prophet said:—The Spirit of God shall rest and dwell upon Him, (a spirit) of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and of courage, of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord. These were the seven eyes that were opened upon the Stone, and these are the seven eyes of the Lord which look upon all the earth.

Here 'who' is taken for 'rare', according to that saying: Who, do you think, is the faithful and wise steward? and: Lord, who dwells in your tabernacle, and who shall go up into your holy mountain?
