Moreover, since the prophet Zechariah exhorts Zion and Jerusalem to a similar gladness, and Matthew says that this very prophecy was fulfilled in the first coming of Christ, we are compelled by necessity, or rather led by the very order of truth, to hope for what is said in Zephaniah not as future but as done. For it is written in Zechariah: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, just and a savior, himself humble and mounted upon a beast of burden and a new colt.

Exult greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king will come to you, just and a savior, himself poor and riding upon a she-ass, and upon a colt, the foal of a she-ass. And I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war shall be scattered, and he shall speak peace to the nations, and his power shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth. LXX: Rejoice exceedingly, daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem: Behold, your king will come to you, just and saving, himself meek and riding upon a beast of burden and a new colt; and he will destroy the chariots from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and he will destroy the bows of the fighters and the multitude, and peace from the nations, and he shall rule over the waters as far as the sea, and the rivers, the outlets of the earth. […]

Now this was done that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, who says: Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting upon an ass and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden. This is written in the prophet Zechariah, of whom it will be spoken more fully in its own place, if span of life is granted. For now we must touch briefly on this: that according to the letter, in the short stretch of the journey, he did not rest sitting upon both animals. For either he sat on the ass and the colt was without a rider, or, if he made use of the colt for sitting (which is more fitting), the ass was led along free. […]

"And Jesus, when He had found a young ass, sat thereon." Here the account is briefly given: for how it all happened may be found at full length in the other evangelists. But there is appended to the circumstance itself a testimony from the prophets, to make it evident that He in whom was fulfilled all they read in Scripture, was entirely misunderstood by the evil-minded rulers of the Jews. Jesus, then, "found a young ass, and sat thereon; as it is written, Fear not, daughter of Zion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass's colt." Among that people, then, was the daughter of Zion to be found; for Zion is the same as Jerusalem. Among that very people, I say, reprobate and blind as they were, was the daughter of Zion, to whom it was said, "Fear not, daughter of Zion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass's colt." […]

Again, although John tells us nothing as to the way in which the Lord despatched His disciples to fetch these animals to Him, nevertheless he inserts a brief allusion to this colt, and cites also the word of the prophet which Matthew makes use of. In the case also of this testimony from the prophet, the terms in which it is reproduced by the evangelists, although they exhibit certain differences, do not fail to express a sense identical in intention. Some difficulty, however, may be felt in the fact that Matthew adduces this passage in a form which represents the prophet to have made mention of the ass; whereas this is not the case, either with the quotation as introduced by John, or with the version given in the ecclesiastical codices of the translation in common use. An explanation of this variation seems to me to be found in the fact that Matthew is understood to have written his Gospel in the Hebrew language. […]
9:9.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 2, Chapter 66

9:9.t: Rejoice greatly O daughter of Sion, shout O daughter of Jerusalem; behold thy King cometh unto thee; he is just and having salvation; lowly and riding upon an ass—even a young colt. This passage he uttered with reference to Zerubabel, in a strain of hyperbole as regards him, for it had properly its accomplishment in the Lord Christ, whom Zerubabel as it were, personified.

9:10.t: For peace and tranquillity of the soul is above all glory of any house; for peace passeth all understanding. This is that peace above all peace which shall be granted after the third shaking of the heaven, the sea, the earth and the dry land, when He shall destroy all Principalities and Powers. For heaven and earth shall pass away, and all the fashion of this world; and every man shall rise up against his brother with the sword, that is, with the word piercing the marrow of the soul, that whatever opposes itself, the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem may be cut off, as Zechariah says. And thus there will be peace over all, the passions of the body offering no resistance, and the unbelieving mind no obstacle, that Christ may be all in all, offering in subjection to the Father the hearts of all men.

And I will destroy, he says, the chariot from Ephraim. It is still spoken in the person of God the Father, that the four-horse chariot, or the chariot, should perish from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem. And meanwhile according to the letter he says this: There shall be no battles, all things having been set at peace by the coming and birth of Christ. Moreover, according to a higher understanding, Ephraim, which is interpreted καρποφορία, that is, fruitfulness and abundance of crops, is referred to the multitude of heresies; of which it is written in Psalm 77 (78): The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle. Of these chariots and cars we read: Some in chariots and some on horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God; they are bound and have fallen, but we have risen and are set upright. The horse that is destroyed from Jerusalem is the one of which we read: A horse is a deceitful thing for safety. […]

9:11.t: The sun was darkened because of the Sun of justice. The rocks were rent because of "the spiritual rock." Tombs were opened, and the dead arose, because of him who was "free among the dead." He "sent forth his prisoners out of the pit, wherein there is no water." Do not be ashamed, then, of the Crucified, but say with confidence, "He bears our sins and carries our sorrows, and by his bruises we are healed." Let us not be ungrateful to our Benefactor. Again, "For the wickedness of my people was he led to death; and I shall give the ungodly for his burial, and the rich for his death." And Paul says clearly "that Christ died for our sins, according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day, according to the Scriptures."

You also, by the blood of your testament, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water; turn to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope; today also, announcing, I will render double to you. LXX: And you, by the blood of the testament, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit that has no water; you shall sit in the stronghold, prisoners of the congregation, and for one day of your sojourning I will render double to you. After the word of the prophet, or rather God the Father Almighty himself, had announced to Zion and Jerusalem that their king was coming to them, meek and mounted upon a she-ass, a beast of burden, and upon the foal of an ass, and that his power would be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth, he makes an apostrophe to Christ himself, of whom the prophecy speaks, and says: You also, by the blood of your testament, or covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water. […]

With this proviso, however, that they interpret the earlier testimony otherwise than we have explained it, and say: O Christ, whom we hope will come, and who are to reign in all the ends of the earth, by the blood of your testament, in which, according to Ezekiel, you found Jerusalem spattered with her own blood, and by which you entered into a covenant with Abraham in the dividing of the calf and the ram and the goat, you have released your people Israel from the captivity and the furnace of the Chaldeans, in whom there was no mercy. Therefore you too, O Israelites, who were prisoners and hoped in the Lord, return to most strongly fortified Jerusalem, for today you have the Lord promising you that for the brief injury of captivity you shall receive all things doubled, as we read that Job also received them.

It was fitting that the herald of his resurrection is reported to have been sitting, so that by sitting he might prefigure him who, having triumphed over the author of death, would ascend to his seat in the everlasting kingdom. Concerning this he said a little later, as he appeared to his disciples, "All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me"; and the evangelist Mark says, "The Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at God's right hand." [The angel] was sitting upon the stone with which the tomb was closed, but which had been rolled away, to teach that [Christ] had cast down and triumphed over the closed places of the lower world by his power, so that he might lift up to the light and the rest of paradise all of his own whom he found there, according to the prophet's [statement], "You also because of the blood of your covenant, have led your prisoners back from the pit, in which there is no water."

But who will deliver us from these plagues? Certainly there is one alone who came to deliver us, namely Christ, who made ten condescensions against the ten plagues. The first was down to our flesh. The second was down to our mortality. The third, to our neediness, for he suffered hunger, thirst, and cold. The fourth was to our poverty, for "he was made destitute," having no place to which he might turn. The fifth, to our temptation, when he permitted himself to be tempted; and in this he bore our weakness. The Apostle: "We do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in all things." The sixth, to the weariness of body and our toil. The seventh, to our anxiety; whence: "Jesus began to be fearful and distressed and said: My soul is sorrowful even unto death." The eighth was to the cross, and this was wondrous. The ninth was to death. The tenth was to the prison of hell.

These are the ten condescensions by which God condescended to man. […]

9:12.t: And again the word is directed to those very ones who were prisoners and who were to be set free by the mercy of Christ: Turn to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope. And the sense is: You who are now prisoners and are held in a harsh and terrible hell, you who hope for the loosing of your bonds at the coming of Christ, turn to the stronghold, or, you shall sit in the stronghold, of which it is written: The fear of the Lord is the bulwark of the holy one, so that you may say: Be to me a God, a protector, and a fortified place, that you may save me; and so that the prophet may also say of you: Behold, a strong city, and our salvation shall set a wall and an outer wall. But this stronghold, to which God exhorts the prisoners of hope, or the hoping prisoners of the Church, we ought to take as nothing other than the dwelling of paradise, into which the thief was the first to enter with the Lord; […]

9:13.t: For I have stretched Judah for myself, as a bow I have filled Ephraim; and I will raise up your sons, O Zion, over your sons, O Greece, and I will set you as the sword of the mighty. LXX: For I have bent you, O Judah, for myself, as a bow I have filled Ephraim; and I will raise up your sons, O Zion, over the sons of the Greeks, and I will handle you as the sword of a warrior. The Jews refer this to the times of the Maccabees, who conquered the Macedonians and, after a space of three and a half years, cleansed the temple that had been defiled by idolatry. And what follows: As a bow I have filled Ephraim, they think signifies those who had come, under Hezekiah, from the ten tribes that are called Israel, over whom Josiah too is recorded to have reigned.

According to tropology this place can be explained thus: Judah is stretched as a bow when the Lord and Savior is sent by the Father into this world, he who is himself both the bow and the archer and the arrow. The bow, as in the present place. The archer, as in Psalm 44 (45): Your arrows are sharp, most mighty; and when someone has been wounded by them, he says: I am wounded with love. And the arrow is he himself who speaks through Isaiah: He has set me as a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he has hidden me. The chosen arrow is the Word of God; the quiver in which the arrow is hidden is the dispensation of the flesh he assumed. With this Ephraim is filled, so that, when he has been armed and made ready for war, he too, together with the nations, may be wounded by the arrows of the Lord; Ephraim, from whose tribe Jeroboam first split the people, whom the prophet Hosea shows more fully to be taken in the person of heretics; […]

9:14.t: And the Lord God shall be seen over them, and his javelin shall go forth like lightning; and the Lord God shall sound the trumpet, and shall go in the whirlwind of the south. The Lord of hosts shall protect them. LXX: And the Lord God shall appear over them; and his arrow shall go forth like lightning; and the Lord God Almighty shall sound with the trumpet, and shall go in the commotion of his terror. The Lord Almighty shall protect them. This place too they refer to the times of the Maccabees: that when these fought against Antiochus and conquered, the fight and the victory were the Lord's, who went forth mighty to battle, and his power appeared like lightning, and, when the adversaries had been conquered and scattered as by a whirlwind, he protected the people of the Jews. We, however, shall refer everything to the understanding of the Savior, of whom it was said above: I have stretched Judah for myself as a bow. […]

9:15.t: Let us speak also according to anagogy, or rather let us explain a prophecy wrapped in many obscurities. The sons of Zion, protected by their Lord, will devour their adversaries, whom we understand as the sons of Greece. And they will subdue them with sling stones, with the threatenings of the Scriptures, making their adversaries subject and humble; for nothing strikes so hard as an example from the holy Scriptures, and a testimony sent forth by the whirl of the mouth. But what is said in the LXX: And they shall drink their blood like wine, we do not read so in the Hebrew, but: Drinking they shall be made drunk as with wine, so that they may hear that word of the Song of Songs: Drink, friends, and be drunk. And so their drunkenness will please like the sacrifice of the altar, and like the horns, or corners, of the altar.

And they shall devour and subdue with sling stones, and drinking they shall be made drunk as with wine, and they shall be filled like bowls, and like the horns of the altar.

And the Lord their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people, because holy stones shall be lifted up over his land. LXX: And they shall consume them, and overwhelm them with sling stones, and they shall drink their blood like wine, and they shall fill the altar like bowls. And the Lord shall save them in that day as sheep, his people, because holy stones shall roll upon his land. For what we have rendered shall be lifted up, and what is written in the Hebrew as methnosasoth, can be interpreted as wandering, or fleeing. […]

9:16.t: The Lord will also save them as the flock of his people, because holy stones shall roll upon his land, stones that will be so light and so striving upward that they will not wait for the hands of the builders, but will themselves hasten to be laid upon the foundation of Christ and to be held together by the cornerstone; of whom the apostle Peter also speaks: As living stones be built up into a spiritual house, and a holy priesthood, offering spiritual victims, pleasing to God. These are the stones that will cry out if the people of the Jews keep silent, and they will roll upon the earth as long as they are in the body, because the earthly habitation weighs down the mind that is anxious about many things; and, set in the flesh, the holy man says: Who will give me wings like a dove? As far as lies in him, he strives and rolls and is raised toward the heights, but he is held back by the frailty of the flesh. […]

This we have said in a general way: but let us speak also in particular of the inner man. The wheel stands upon the earth with only some small trace of contact, and it not only stands, but as it were runs on: it does not stand still, but touches and passes by: finally, when it is rolled, it always mounts up to higher things. So too the holy man, because he is in the body, has the necessity of thinking some things about earthly matters; and when he has come to food and clothing and the rest of such things, having food and clothing, with these he is content, touching the earth, and he hastens to higher things. In him who runs and hastens to higher things, in him is your word. We read also in the prophet: "Holy stones are rolled upon the earth." See what he said: Holy stones are rolled upon the earth. For because they are wheels, therefore they are rolled upon the earth and hasten to higher things.

9:17.t: For what is his goodness, and what is his beauty, but the grain of the elect, and wine that makes virgins spring forth? LXX: For if there is anything best of his, and if anything good from him, grain for young men and wine of good odor for virgins. Therefore, they say, the Maccabees, fleeing hither and thither, will overcome with the Lord's help, so that, when the Macedonians have been cast out of the land of Israel, the temple may be cleansed, the precepts of the law may be kept, and the learning of the Scriptures may again make virgins spring forth, that is, peoples believing in one God, who before had been defiled by the worship of idolatry. By the grain of the elect, that is, baurim, they would have us understand not young men, as the Seventy translated, but chosen and learned men, who are found worthy to eat the grain, that is, the law of God. For wine, which in Hebrew is called thiros, Aquila translated οἰνίαν (vintage), which itself also can be referred to the abundance of the vintage. So the Jews think. […]

10:1.t: Ask of the Lord rain in the late season, and the Lord will make snows and will give them showers of rain, to each one grass in the field. For the idols have spoken what is useless, and the diviners have seen a lie, and the dreamers have spoken in vain, they comforted vainly; therefore they have been led away like a flock, they shall be afflicted, because they have no shepherd. LXX: Ask rain of the Lord in due season, early and late. The Lord has made phantasies, and he will give them winter rain, to each one grass in the field, for those who spoke have spoken troubles; and the diviners false visions, and they have spoken false dreams, they comforted vainly; therefore they have been dried up like sheep, and they have been afflicted because there was none to heal. […]

But according to the spiritual understanding we can say that the Lord exhorts those who believe in Christ to ask for the late rain at the consummation of the world, when the fullness of grace is to be given, and grass will grow up for each one in his own field, so that they may be able to say: The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture, there he has set me, beside the waters of refreshment he has brought me up.

10:2.t: Or else Israel itself, which was once deceived and held fast by the errors of idolatry, may understand that it worshipped idols in vain, and listened to the lies of diviners, and acquiesced in dreams, which Scripture commands us not to believe. And for this reason they were led like a flock into captivity, and afflicted, without God as their shepherd, because they did not have knowledge of the law. This whole place is obscure and doubtful, and the reader ought to pardon us if, in things that are ambiguous, we too walk with a hesitant step.

For all the idols, and the diviners and the dreamers, have spoken in vain, and comforted vainly. These things he says of the heretics, who under the Christian name understand neither what they are saying nor what they are affirming, and who give heed to erring spirits and to teachers of demons who speak lies in hypocrisy, and have their conscience seared, so that, being by no means believers, they are led away by the consolations of those who promise vain things; and for this reason they have been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and led away into the captivity of the king of Babylon, and they shall be afflicted, because they do not have Christ as their shepherd, whom they promise themselves under a false name.

10:3.t: My fury is angered against the shepherds, and I will visit upon the he-goats; for the Lord of hosts has visited his flock, the house of Judah, and has made them like the horse of his glory in war. From him the corner, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle, from him shall go forth every exactor together; and they shall be like mighty men treading down the mire of the streets in battle, and they shall fight, because the Lord is with them. LXX: My fury is stirred up against the shepherds, and I will visit upon the lambs; and the Lord God Almighty will visit his flock, the house of Judah, and will make them like his comely horse in battle; and from him he looked, and from him he set, and from him the bow in fury, there shall go forth everyone who goes forth together, and they shall be like warriors treading down the mire of the streets in battle, and they shall be made ready, because the Lord is with them. In this place too the Jews have a twofold exposition. […]

Our writers, however, refer these things to the times of persecution, because for the fault of the priests the people too is often handed over to its adversaries; and yet the Lord Almighty afterwards visits his flock, the house of Judah, which confesses God both in word and in mind, and makes them like the horse of his glory in war, of which the saints say: Mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.

It was their duty to have known the meaning of what had been spoken of old, as being before decreed by God concerning them. For among others are words like these, "My wrath is kindled against the shepherds, and I will visit the lambs." For the wicked shepherds perished miserably: while the calling of those who were obedient to salvation was a kind of visitation; for a remnant of Israel was saved.
10:3.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

10:4.t: He himself will also be the bow of the Lord's fury, of which he says: I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and again: My arrows shall consume them. Of this bow, and of these arrows, we read in Psalm 7: He has bent his bow and made it ready, and on it he has made ready the instruments of death; he has made his arrows for the burning.

And what follows: From him the corner, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle, from him shall go forth every exactor together, they understand μεταφορικῶς (metaphorically), so that they interpret the corner as the royal power, because it holds the walls together. And from him, he says, the peg, that is, the priesthood. Read Isaiah, in whom Eliakim is fastened in the temple of God like a peg. From him the bow of battle: men strong for war; from him also every exactor together, which in the Hebrew is written noges, and Aquila translated εἰσπράσσων (exactor), so that not only were there strong and good men, but others among them were unworthy of their lineage. […]

10:5.t: And they shall tread down, he says, their adversaries, crowned in martyrdom, and they shall say: The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life, of whom shall I be afraid? While the wicked drew near against me to eat my flesh, my enemies who trouble me, they themselves were weakened and fell. Though camps should stand together against me, my heart shall not fear; though battle should rise up against me, in this will I hope. Then shall that saying be fulfilled: One of you shall pursue a thousand, and two shall put many thousands to flight.

This can be explained according to tropology thus. When the Lord Almighty visits his flock, the house of Judah, then the riders on horses shall be confounded, of whom it is written: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea. Of whom it is also sung in the voice of the psalmist: At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, they who mounted horses have slumbered. And the choir of the saints redoubles it: Some in chariots, and some on horses, but we will call upon the name of our God; they have been bound and have fallen, but we have risen and stand upright. In this cavalry the king of Egypt trusted; and, hurled headlong into the sea, he sank like lead into the depths, and learned by his own example that what is written is true: A horse is a deceitful thing for safety. These chariots and four-horse teams we interpreted above as the four passions, which, unless they are governed by the reins of a good charioteer, are carried over the precipice. […]

And the riders on horses shall be confounded.

And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph; and I will bring them back, because I will have mercy on them; and they shall be as they were when I had not cast them off, for I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them. And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim, and their heart shall rejoice as from wine; and their sons shall see and shall rejoice; and their heart shall exult in the Lord. LXX: And the riders on horses shall be confounded, and I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will make them dwell, because I have loved them. And they shall be as when I had not cast them away, for I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them; and they shall be like the warriors of Ephraim, and their heart shall rejoice as in wine, and their sons shall see and shall rejoice, and their heart shall be glad in the Lord. […]

10:6.t: Then God says that he strengthens the house of Judah and the house of Joseph, so that those who were divided while Jeroboam reigned may be united while Christ rules, and there may be one shepherd and one flock. For both Judah and Joseph, under different names, are brought together into the one understanding of the Savior, because Joseph lavished grain on the peoples hungering in Egypt, and the Lord satisfied the hunger of the world with his presence. And he will bring them back, and will have mercy on them, and so they shall be one, as they were before he cast them off. Take all these things of the persecutions, when, all hope being lost, the Lord heard his servants.

10:7.t: And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim, who, at first weak and infirm, shall afterwards be mighty and worthy of their name. For Ephraim is interpreted fruitfulness. And their heart shall rejoice when they have drunk the wine that was pressed from the vine of Sorek. Their sons also, to whom the apostle Paul speaks: My little sons, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you. And Peter, the prince of the apostles: As sons, he says, of obedience, not conformed according to your former manner of life. And in the psalm we read: Come, sons, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. These sons, therefore, shall exult and rejoice, and their heart shall be glad in the Lord.

10:8.t: According to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), the Lord signals and whistles to those who had before been captives to sins, and speaks to them: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and you shall find rest for your souls. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden is light. What is more merciful than this signal and whistle, by which the scattered people is gathered? And they are gathered because the Lord has redeemed them, not with corruptible silver and gold, from their vain manner of life, but with the precious blood, as of a spotless lamb, the Lord Jesus. Hence he speaks in the psalm: My exultation, deliver me from those who surround me, and again: You have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth. And he will multiply them as they had been multiplied before, so that what was promised to Abraham might be fulfilled: I will multiply him and I will bless him, and he shall be blessed, so that he may become the father of many nations. […]

I will whistle for them, and I will gather them, because I have redeemed them, and I will multiply them as they had been multiplied before. And I will sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me, and they shall live with their sons, and shall return. And I will bring them back from the land of Egypt, and from the Assyrians I will gather them, and I will lead them to the land of Gilead and of Lebanon, and room shall not be found for them. LXX: I will signal to them, and I will receive them, because I will redeem them, and they shall be multiplied as they were very many, and I will sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me. They shall nourish their sons and shall turn back, and I will bring them back from the land of Egypt, and from the Assyrians I will receive them, and into Galaaditis and into Lebanon I will bring them, and none of them shall be lacking. […]

Of them in sooth He said by the voice of Isaiah, "I will make signs unto them, and receive them, because I will ransom them, and they shall be multiplied, as they were many: and I will sow them among the nations, and they who are afar off shall remember Me." For very many were they that were astray, but were called through Christ: and again they are many as they were before; for they have been received and ransomed, having obtained as the token of peace from God the Father, the adoption into His family and the grace that is by faith in Jesus Christ. And the divine disciples were sown widely among the nations: and what is the consequence? Those who in disposition were far from God, have been made near. To whom also the divine Paul sends an epistle, saying, "Now ye who some time were afar off have been made near in the blood of Christ."
10:8.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

10:9.t: In short, there follows: I will sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me. They who heard the word of the Lord were sown among the peoples: Go, teach all nations, and in another place: You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and I have appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and your fruit should remain forever. And when the apostles have been sown among the peoples, the nations and peoples set far off shall remember me, that prophetic word agreeing with this saying: All the ends of the earth shall remember and shall turn to the Lord. And all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight. For the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations. And what is said: From afar they shall remember me, is like this: You who are far off, remember the Lord, and let Jerusalem come up upon your heart. The whole multitude of the nations was far off, but it remembered God, because we are all begotten of one parent. […]

10:10.t: And I will bring them back, he says, from the land of Egypt, and from the Assyrians I will gather them. From the land of Egypt, in which King Pharaoh ruled, who once said boastfully: The rivers are mine, and I made them. And from the land of Asshur, which the king of Assyria held, the great mind, who himself also said: Above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High. And when the Lord has gathered the nations from the darkness of Egypt, and from the tribulation of the world, and from the power of the Assyrian, who is interpreted 'reproving and convicting', for he is the enemy and the avenger, he will lead them into the land of Gilead and of Lebanon. Gilead, turned into our language, is 'the testimony of migration', when we pass over from carnal things to spiritual, come from the part to the whole, leave earthly things behind and migrate to the heavenly. And Lebanon is interpreted λευκασμὸς, that is, whitening. […]

10:11.t: For the rest, we who are reckoned by the name of Christ leave behind the letter that kills and follow the spirit that gives life, or rather, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we look not for the Bosporus, and the drying of the sea once more, and the dry streams of the Jordan, which are like fables, but for the worthy mercy of God toward his servants, by which, as he goes before and opens the way for us, we pass through the strait of the sea, or the narrow sea, which for sinners is very broad: For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, strait and narrow the way that leads to life. Of this sea we also read in the psalms: They who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters, they have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep. Into this sea of the world, in which the number of the saints is hemmed in and set in tribulation, the apostles went down, and first of all the Lord, that he might free us from the bitter waves. […]

And he shall pass through the strait of the sea, and shall strike the waves in the sea; and all the depths of the river shall be confounded, and the pride of Asshur shall be humbled, and the scepter of Egypt shall depart. I will strengthen them in the Lord, and in his name they shall walk, says the Lord. LXX: And they shall pass through in the narrow sea, and they shall strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the rivers shall be dried up; and all the injury of the Assyrians shall be taken away, and the scepter of Egypt shall be removed. And I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, and in his name they shall glory, says the Lord. […]

And when they have passed through the strait of the sea, and have trodden its waves under their foot, all the depths of the river shall be confounded, of which it is written: He who turns the sea into dry land; they shall pass through the river on foot; so that the pride, or the injury, of Asshur may be humbled, and the dominion of Egypt may depart from the saints and believers, and those who have been freed may be strengthened in the Lord and say: My strength and my praise is the Lord, and again: I will love you, O Lord, my strength, and with Jeremiah: My strength and my help and my refuge, O Lord my God.

10:12.t: Hence the Apostle too, in whom Christ was speaking, said: I can do all things in him who strengthens me; and not only shall they be strengthened in the Lord, but they shall also glory in him and say: But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world, and: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord, and in another place: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: to understand and know the Lord, and to do mercy and judgment in the midst of the earth. But since in the Hebrew it is written: And in his name they shall walk, it is to be understood thus: that Christians walk in the name of Christ, and a new name is written on their pebbles, and under the dignity of so great a name they walk with the Lord, as Enoch walked, and pleased God, and was translated.

11:1.t:
And when did Jerusalem after its siege by the Babylonians undergo a second burning, and have its Temple thrown to the ground?

And the figure used by the prophet is also exceedingly strange when he says, "O Libanus, open thy gates, and let fire devour thy cedars." For he calls the Temple here, as was not unusual, by the name of Libanus (it is so called in other prophecies). To this the Jews themselves now assent, since Isaiah, too, has a similar prophecy to the one before us, namely:

"Behold, the Lord of Sabaoth shall disturb the noble with might, and the lofty shall be crushed in their pride." And Libanus shall fall with its lofty ones, and there shall come forth a rod from the stem of Jesse, and a flower shall spring up from his roots, and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him."

To which he adds:

"And there shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to rule the Gentiles, in him shall the Gentiles trust." […]
11:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 4

11:1.t: Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Howl, O fir tree, for the cedar has fallen, because the magnificent have been laid waste. Howl, O oaks of Bashan, because the fortified forest has been cut down. LXX: Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Let the pine howl, for the cedar has fallen, for the nobles have been crushed. Howl, O oaks of Bashanitis, because the wooded forest has been brought down. Plainly Lebanon, to which the prophetic word turns, saying: Open your gates, O Lebanon, is understood as the temple of the Jews, which, restored, or rather built, by Zerubbabel, is sung as destined to be overthrown again by Vespasian and Titus. And because he had called the temple Lebanon μεταφορικῶς (metaphorically), he keeps the figure in the rest as well, so that by the cedars and fir trees and oaks of Bashan and the wooded forest he signifies the princes and priests and people of the Jews. […]

Some, not understanding this place, refer Lebanon and the fir trees and pines and the oaks of Bashan, and the wooded or fortified forest, to the opposing powers, of which it is also said in Ezekiel, under the name of Asshur and of Pharaoh: Behold, Asshur was a cypress on Lebanon, fair in its branches, and thick with shade, and lofty in its height, and its top was among the clouds; water nourished it, the abyss raised it on high, and the rest, which are said both of Asshur and of Pharaoh, and they think these are said either of the opposing powers, or of all the proud and the princes, of whom we also read in the psalm: The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars, and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and in another place: The day of the Lord Sabaoth upon everyone who is insolent and proud, and upon everyone who is lofty and exalted, and a little after: And upon every cedar of Lebanon that is lofty, and upon every oak tree of Bashan. […]

11:2.t: Look also, I pray you, at those who stretch themselves upon beds of ivory, whom the divine Amos fitly upbraids, who anoint themselves with the chief ointments, and chant to the sound of instruments of music, and attach themselves to transitory things as though they were stable, but have not grieved nor had compassion for the affliction of Joseph; though they ought to have been kind to those who had met with disaster before them, and by mercy have obtained mercy; as the fir-tree should howl, because the cedar had fallen, and be instructed by their neighbours' chastisement, and be led by others' ills to regulate their own lives, having the advantage of being saved by their predecessors' fate, instead of being themselves a warning to others.

The fir trees howl because the cedar has fallen, the princes and priests mourning one another in their own devastation. And what he said obscurely before, he now sets out more plainly: Because the magnificent have been laid waste. I want to know what are the cedars of Lebanon that were burned, what are the fir trees to which howling is enjoined, what is the pine that has fallen; the magnificent, he says, have been laid waste. Howl, O oaks of Bashan, that is, of confusion and ignominy, because the most fortified forest, which in Hebrew is called besor, and was translated by the LXX as wooded, has been cut down; because the temple, which had grown up in impregnable strength, and had been built by various kings and princes, and afterwards by Herod, was destroyed when the Roman attacked it.

11:3.t: The voice of the howling of the shepherds, because their magnificence is laid waste; the voice of the roaring of lions, because the pride of the Jordan is laid waste. LXX: The voice of shepherds mourning, since their magnificence has been made wretched. The voice of lions roaring, because the roaring of the Jordan is afflicted. Part of the preceding passage is contained in these little verses too. Those whom he had called cedars, firs, pines and oaks of Bashan — and, explaining what these trees were, he had added, saying: Since the magnificent are laid waste — he now, by another μεταφορὰν (metaphor), says are shepherds, that is, princes and teachers; and those who were first among the people, he says, ought to weep and mourn, because their magnificence and beauty and glory has been laid waste and consumed, namely the temple, in which they gloried. And the voice, he says, of the roaring of lions: those whom he calls lofty trees, and again shepherds, the same he now calls lions. […]

And, as if already, so to speak, they had fallen into ruin and destruction, and were wailing and weeping on this account, the prophet hoard, he says, "the voice of shepherds wailing, because their might was brought low: the voice of lions roaring, because the pride of Jordan was spoiled." He calls the lions the pride of Jordan, by whom wore figured the chiefs of the Jewish synagogue: who, in just requital of their wickedness against Christ, wailed with their fathers and children, being consumed as with fire and sword, while the temple at Jerusalem was also burnt, and the cities throughout all Judaea abandoned to utter desolation.
11:3.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

11:4.t: Thus says the Lord my God: Feed the cattle of slaughter, which those who had possessed them were killing, and were not grieving; and they were selling them, saying: Blessed be the Lord, we have become rich; and their shepherds were not sparing them. LXX: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Feed the sheep of slaughter, which those who possessed them were killing, and they did not repent; and those who were selling them were saying: Blessed be the Lord, and we have become rich; and their shepherds suffered nothing over them. Where the prophecy is most manifest, and through the metaphor the true order of the history is narrated, the interpretation of tropology is superfluous: that we should say that some shepherds are good and others bad, and refer this as much to the old people as to the new, that is, as much to the priests and princes of the Jews as to the bishops and presbyters of the Christians; […]

11:6.t: Because, then, their shepherds were not sparing them, and they themselves were the first to devour my people, therefore I too will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land of Judea, says the Lord. For he speaks of this land, of which his discourse was, and not of the whole world, as the Jews, interpreting badly, wish to twist God's sentence away from themselves in another direction. For after the overthrow of the temple — which befell them for this reason, that for forty-two years after the Lord suffered, though granted a space of time, they would not repent —, I will let loose, he says, each one against his neighbor; and they will cut one another down in mutual slaughter, or else in the very siege of the temple, when the Roman army shall surround Jerusalem; for there will be such wars and discords among the Jews themselves that the people will be divided into three parts. […]

11:7.t:
But if the price of Him that was valued, there cast down rendered the House profane, it is natural for Him to proceed to say, "And I cast the second rod, the Rope, to break the covenant between Judah and Israel."

For from that day the multitude of the nation was cut away from God's ancient providential guardianship. And I suppose the second rod to mean the whole Jewish nation. It is therefore called a Rope in the words, "The one I called Beauty, and the other I called a Rope." And he proceeds to speak clearly of the second: "And I cast away the second rod, the Rope, to break my covenant between Judah and Israel." For they were the Rope and the second rod. But the first rod, called Beauty, was Jerusalem itself, and the Mosaic Worship, and the whole of the old covenant. This is shewn by the prophecy, saying, "And I will take my rod of beauty, and I will cast it away, to break my covenant." […]
11:7.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 4

11:7.t: And I will no longer spare those who dwell on the land, says the Lord. Behold, I will deliver men, each one into the hand of his neighbor, and into the hand of his king; and they shall cut down the land, and I will not rescue from their hand; and I will feed the cattle of slaughter for this, O poor of the flock. LXX: Therefore I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. And behold, I will deliver men, each one into the hands of his neighbor, and into the hand of his kings; and they shall cut down the land, and I will not rescue from their hand, and I will feed the sheep of slaughter in Canaanitis. What the LXX translated at the end of the passage: And I will feed the sheep of slaughter in the land of Canaan, is not in the Hebrew, and is translated by none of the other translators.

And I will feed the cattle of slaughter, so that the Jews may always be nourished for death; because this is the sentence of God: O you who are the poor of the flock, that is, the just of Israel, who have believed in the Lord Jesus and received the Son of God, hear what is said, and learn the mysteries of the following passage. But what we read according to the Seventy: And I will feed the sheep of slaughter in the land of Canaan, we can understand thus: that the Lord feeds the people of the Jews, which is destined for death and scattered through the whole world — that is, in the land of Canaan and of the Gentiles —, and nourishes it for sacrifice.

The Creator and shepherd, whose sheep know his voice and follow him, took for himself two staffs, or two σκυτάλας, that is, sticks, which in Hebrew are called macaloth, to show the bearing of a shepherd. One staff he called Beauty: that is, under Noah he protected the whole human race with his blessing, when, the world being restored, sins had not yet made it foul. And therefore the calling of all the nations is called beautiful and fair, because nothing is more just than that the parent of the universe should call all equally, whom he begot in equal condition. And the other he called Cords; for when the Most High was dividing the nations and scattering the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of the Lord. And his people Jacob became the portion of the Lord; Israel the cord of his inheritance. And I fed, he says, the flock: either Israel itself, or, together with Israel, the whole human race.

Some have understood the two callings as those of the Jews and of the Gentiles: by the first name Israel, and by the last the Christians. But how the Christian calling was cast away first, and the Jews remained and were fed by God, they did not sufficiently consider.

And I took for myself two staffs: one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cords; and I fed the flock.

And I cut off three shepherds in one month, and my soul was straitened over them, since their soul also varied against me. And I said: I will not feed you; what dies, let it die, and what is cut off, let it be cut off, and let the rest devour each one the flesh of his neighbor. LXX: And I will take for myself two staffs: one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord; and I will feed the sheep. And I will take away three shepherds in one month, and my soul will grow heavy upon them, since their souls also were roaring against me. And I said: I will not feed them; what dies, let it die, and what fails, let it fail, and let the rest devour each one the flesh of his neighbor. Above he had said: For this, O poor of the flock; […]

11:8.t: And when the prophecy goes on to say, "And I will take away three shepherds in one month," I think that it refers to the three divisions of the ancient leaders of the people of God—the King, the Prophet, and the High-Priest—for by those three shepherds all the affairs of the ancients were managed. But since those three offices were destroyed together in our Saviour's time—(for their king reigned not in accordance with the Law, being a foreigner and not a member of the Jewish race; their high-priest was appointed to his office by the Romans, and did not attain his rank by the order of succession of the tribe, nor according to lawful custom; […]
11:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 4

11:8.t: And I cut off, he says, three shepherds in one month. I have read in the commentaries of a certain writer that the shepherds cut off by the Lord's indignation are to be understood as the priests and false prophets and kings of the Jews; because after the passion of Christ all were cut off at one time, those of whom Jeremiah speaks: The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? Those who held my law did not know me. And the shepherds transgressed against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal, and followed idols. Not content with this explanation, he wants the three shepherds cut off in one month to be taken as those who have sinned against the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; for all heretics sin either against one, or against two, or against three persons at once. Let him have said what he wished, for one must not detract from another's sense. To us the three shepherds who were cut off in one month seem to be Moses, and Aaron, and Miriam; […]

Let us understand this according to the letter of Moses and Aaron. Moses indeed was led out, and Aaron, but not led into the land of promise. Jesus succeeded him. See what is written. Moses died in the desert, Aaron died, Miriam died; and this is what is written in the prophet: "And I will strike," it says, "three shepherds in one month." They died: for they could not enter into the land of promise. They only saw over against the land of promise, and could not enter.

11:9.t: Wherefore in indignation I said to Moses: I will not feed you; let me alone and I will destroy them. But when, in anger, he says, let me alone, he invites entreaty, and shows that he can be held back by him. What dies, he says, let it die, and what is cut off, let it be cut off; let the bodies of all fall in the wilderness, and, turned to sedition, let them be torn by one another's bites like beasts, and let none enter the land of promise.

11:10.t: And I took my staff which was called Beauty, and I cut it off, to make void my covenant which I had struck with all peoples. And it was made void on that day, and thus the poor of the flock who keep watch for me knew that it is the word of the Lord. LXX: And I will take my fair staff, and I will cast it away, to scatter my testament which I disposed toward all peoples; and it shall be scattered on that day, and the Canaanites shall know, the sheep that are kept for me, that it is the word of the Lord. After the calling of Israel, and the taking up of the second staff, which was called Cord, the Lord took the first staff, the nations of the whole world, which were called beautiful, and cut them off from his worship, because they venerated idols, and all have turned aside, together they have become useless. And setting out more plainly what this staff was, he added: To make void my covenant which I had struck with all peoples. For as soon as Israel was taken up, the crowd of the nations was cast away; […]

11:11.t: And as the oracle intended clearly their destruction by this, it naturally goes on to say that they shall no longer recognize the power of things prophesied, but the Canaanites will, when He says, "And the Canaanites shall know, my sheep kept for me, because it is the Word of the Lord." Who are meant by the Canaanites but ourselves, who once were foreigners, and sheep kept for Christ from all the old heathen and sinful nations? We that have been converted by His grace, and understanding the things prophesied, have received the true knowledge of the word of the Lord; yea, we Canaanites know and understand what was meant; but they that boasted of Israel, and gloried in being of the seed of Abraham, neither knew nor understood.
11:11.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 4

11:11.t: And it was made void, he says, my covenant which I had entered into with all the nations. And the poor of the flock understood, that is, the people Israel which keeps my commands, that it is the word of the Lord, that is, that it is the Lord's will to cast off the nations that deny, and in Abraham to take up Israel that confesses. For what we have translated: And thus the poor of the flock knew, the Seventy translated: And the Canaanites shall know, the sheep that are kept for me, which some expound thus: The people of the Jews shall know, to whom it was said: Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah, which is now kept by my ceremonies; or else, because Canaanites is interpreted 'ready for humiliation', those shall know who were once made ready to be humbled by the Lord and to be abandoned. But why, for what we have translated: Thus the poor, they said: Canaanites, the cause is manifest; for among the Hebrews 'thus' is called chen, 'poor' anie; […]

11:12.t: But since what the evangelist says after these things (then was fulfilled that which had been spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying the things which are written) — this is not found to have been prophesied by Jeremiah anywhere in his books, whether those which are read in the churches or those which are recited among the Jews — but if anyone can know, let him show where it is written. I suspect, however, that either it is an error of the Scripture and Jeremiah is put for Zechariah, or that there is some secret writing of Jeremiah in which it is written. Now such is the text in Zechariah the prophet: "and I will say to them: if it is good in your sight, give me my wages, or refuse them; and they appointed my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: put them down into the furnace, and see if it is genuine, even as I was proved for their sake. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and put them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace". […]

[Passage quoted, Zech. xi. 7b-14.]

THIS was fulfilled when, according to Luke:

"Judas went away, and spoke with the chief priests and scribes and captains of the Temple, that he might betray him unto them. And they were glad, and covenanted to give him money;"

or, according to Mark when, "he went to the chief priests to betray him; and they were glad and promised to give him money." In each case it is simply money that is named. But in Matthew the amount is recorded, and it agrees with the quotation from Zechariah. For Matthew says:

"Then went one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, to the chief priests, and said to them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? and they weighed unto him thirty staters."

And this agrees with, "And they weighed my price thirty pieces of silver," spoken by the Lord in the prophecy.

And there is added to this, "And the Lord said to me, Drop them into the furnace, and see if it is good metal, as I was tested by them." […]
11:12.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 4

11:12.t: Hear now in regard to thirty pieces of silver: "And I will say to them, 'If it seems good to you, give me my wages, or refuse.' " One recompense is due me for curing the blind and the lame, and I receive another; instead of thanksgiving, dishonor, and instead of worship, insult. Do you see how Scripture foresaw all this? "And they counted out my wages, thirty pieces of silver." O prophetic accuracy! A great and unerring wisdom of the Holy Spirit! For he did not say ten or twenty but thirty, exactly the right amount. Tell also what happened to this payment, O prophet! Does he who received it keep it, or does he give it back? And after its return what becomes of it? The prophet says, "So I took thirty pieces of silver, and I cast them into the house of the Lord, into the foundry." Compare with the prophecy of the Gospel, which says, "Judas repented and flung the pieces of silver into the temple and withdrew."

And I said to them: If it is good in your eyes, bring my wage, and if not, be still; and they weighed out my wage, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: Cast them to the statuary, the fine price at which I was priced by them; and I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them into the house of the Lord to the statuary. LXX: And I will say to them: If it is good in your sight, give, setting my wage, or refuse. And they set my wage, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: Put them down into the furnace, and consider whether it is tested, as I was tested for them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and put them into the house of the Lord into the furnace. Since the poor of the Israelite flock, who keep my commands, knew that what I spoke was the word of the Lord, and that what I said was true — what I said, that is, to the poor of the flock: If it pleases you; […]

The Jews, interpreting this place maliciously, relate the thirty pieces of silver to thirty commands of the law which they are ordered to do in the law, and again thirty-six others which are forbidden in the law; and they say that they are told to return the silver of the Lord's commands to their modeller and moulder, God, and that because they would not do it, they were cast away. I wished to indicate briefly what they think; otherwise it is wearisome to unroll their most long-winded explanation, so that we may pass on to the rest.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one valued, whom they valued from the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed for me. This testimony is not found in Jeremiah; but in Zechariah, who is almost the last of the twelve prophets, a certain likeness is reported, and although the sense does not differ much, yet both the order and the words are different. I read recently, in a certain Hebrew volume which a Hebrew of the Nazarene sect brought to me, an apocryphal Jeremiah, in which I found these things written word for word. But still it seems to me that the testimony is rather taken from Zechariah, in the common manner of the evangelists and apostles, who, passing over the order of the words, bring forward only the sense from the Old Testament as an example.

And thus it is that Matthew here relates what took place between Pilate and the Lord.

First, however, he makes a digression with the purpose of telling the story of Judas' end, which is related only by him. His account is in these terms: "Then Judas, which had betrayed Him, when he saw that He was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, I have sinned, in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? See thou to that. And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself. And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in. Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day. […]
11:12.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 3, Chapter 7

11:13.t: And the Lord said to me, says the prophet, or else the Savior himself, whose are the preceding words, bearing witness that the Father spoke to him: Cast it to the statuary, for which in the Hebrew is read ioser, that is, τὸν πλάστην, whom we can call moulder and potter. And the sense is: Cast my price to the potter, who is the Creator and moulder of all. Nor did he say, put it down, but cast it, so that the wage of the Lord might be weighed by the judgment of the moulder and modeller. And εἰρονικῶς (ironically), seeing his price, that is, the price of the divine majesty, in thirty pieces of silver, and himself betrayed for so cheap a wage: A fine price, he says, at which I was priced by them; and this must be read with more emphasis, with the mockery and derision of the speaker: At so much did my people, once the poor of the flock and chosen by me as sons, judge that I should be bought and sold! […]

11:14.t: And I cut off my second staff, which was called Cord, so that I might dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. LXX: And I cast away the second staff, which was called Cord, so that I might scatter the covenant that was between Judah and Israel. In this place too I know that I have read a long explanation by a certain writer, or rather inextricable tangles, who brings forward from the book of Ezekiel the two staffs joined into one fellowship, and fits to this passage everything that is to be understood spiritually about the concord of Judah and Ephraim. But let us follow the order we have begun. After the Lord was crucified by the Jews and valued at thirty pieces of silver, and the price of his blood availed for the burial of the Gentiles, who were strangers to the law and the commandments of God, at once the Lord, no longer putting off his sentence, says: I cut off my second staff, which was properly mine, which clung to me in such a way that in Jeremiah it was called a loincloth and a girdle and a […]

11:15.t: O shepherds, disciples of the Lord, feed the flock and lead (it) well! Strengthen the sick, support the weak, bind up the broken, make whole the lame, and take heed to the fattened ones for the Lord of the flock. Be not likened unto an unskilled and foolish shepherd, who in his foolishness is not able to feed the flock, and whose arm is dried up, and whose eye has been blinded, because he said: "dying, let it die; and perishing, let it perish, and the flesh that is left shall be eaten by its companions ". And when the Chief of the shepherds comes He will condemn the unskilled and foolish shepherd who has not cared well for his fellow servants. And he who has shepherded the flock and led (it) well shall be called "a good and skillful servant" (cf. S. Mt. 25: 21), who has presented the flock to the Shepherd while it was intact.

O stupid and foolish pastor, to whose right hand and to whose right eye I committed my sheep. Because thou didst say concerning the sheep, let that which dieth, die, and let that which perisheth perish, and whatever is left, let them devour the flesh of one another; therefore, behold I will make blind thy right eye and I will wither up thy right arm. Thy eye which regarded a bribe shall be blinded, and thy hand which did not rule in righteousness shall waste away.

And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself yet again the instruments of a foolish shepherd. For behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, who will not visit what is forsaken, will not seek what is scattered, and will not heal what is broken, and will not nourish what stands, and he will eat the flesh of the fat ones and break apart their hooves. O shepherd and idol, forsaking the flock, a sword upon his arm and upon his right eye; his arm shall be dried up with withering, and his right eye, growing dark, shall be darkened. LXX: And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself yet again the shepherd's instruments of an unskilled shepherd. For behold, I will raise up a shepherd upon the land, who shall not visit what is forsaken and shall not seek out what is scattered, and shall not heal what is broken, and shall not guide what is whole, and shall devour the flesh of the choice ones, and twist their ankles. O you who pasture vain things, and who have forsaken the sheep, a sword upon his arm, and upon his right eye; […]

11:16.t: This shepherd will rise up in Israel for this reason, because the true shepherd had said: I will no longer feed you. Under another name, both in the prophet Daniel and in the Gospel and in Paul's epistle to the Thessalonians, he is prophesied as the abomination of desolation, who is to sit in the temple of the Lord and make himself out to be God; and through Isaiah too he is called the great mind. And he comes for this, not to heal but to destroy the flock of Israel. For the good shepherd visits the sick animals, seeks out the scattered, brings back those left behind, supports the weary. On the contrary, the bad shepherd does everything the opposite way, and having devoured the flesh of the fat ones, he breaks apart and twists the hooves of the rams and the sheep, so that they may not walk with a straight foot. […]

11:17.t: Having described the worst shepherd, foolish and unskilled, the prophetic discourse turns to the shepherd himself: O shepherd and idol. So wicked is the shepherd that he is called not a worshiper of idols but himself an idol, since he calls himself God and wishes to be adored by all. He forsook the flock to be devoured by beasts, the flock which the Lord had guarded for so long a time. A sword upon his arm, and his strength, and upon his right eye, by which he boasted that he keenly discerned the mysteries of God and saw more than all the prophets before him had seen, so much so that he called himself the Son of God. And that sword is the one of which we both learn above and shall now speak in part, the one of which Isaiah too speaks: My sword has been made drunk in heaven. […]

12:1.t: There are many statements of spirit in general in the sacred Scriptures, and a person could easily become confused from ignorance, if he did not know to what sort of spirit the particular text refers; therefore we must be sure of the nature of the Holy Spirit according to Scripture. For example, Aaron is called Christ (anointed), and David also, and Saul and others are called christs, yet there is only one true Christ; similarly, since the name of spirit has been given to many things, we must determine what in particular is called the Holy Spirit. Many things are called spirits; our soul is called spirit; this wind, which is blowing, is called spirit; great valor is called spirit; impure action is called spirit; and a hostile devil is called spirit. Take care, therefore, when you hear such things, not to mistake one for another because of the similarity of the name. Scripture says of the soul, "When his spirit departs, he returns to the earth"; and again of the soul: "Who forms the spirit of man within him."

Therefore he referred the thunders to the words of the Lord, the sound of which went out into all the earth. And we understand the word spirit in this place of the soul, which he took endowed with potential reason and perfection. For the Scripture often designates the soul of humankind by the word spirit, as you read: "Who creates the spirit of man within him." So too the Lord signified his soul by the word spirit, when he said, "Into your hands I commend my spirit."

The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel. The Lord said, stretching out the heaven and founding the earth and forming the spirit of man within him: Behold, I will make Jerusalem a lintel of drunkenness for all the peoples round about; but Judah too shall be in the siege against Jerusalem. And it shall be: on that day: I will make Jerusalem a stone of burden for all the peoples; all who have lifted it shall be torn with gashing, and all the nations of the earth shall be gathered against her. LXX: The taking up of the word of the Lord upon Israel. The Lord says, stretching out the heaven and founding the earth, and forming the spirit of man within him: Behold, I will make Jerusalem like lintels that are shaken for all the peoples round about, and in Judea. And there shall be a siege around Jerusalem, and it shall be on that day, I will make Jerusalem a stone that is trodden down by all the nations; everyone who treads her down, mocking shall mock, and I will gather against her all the nations of the earth. […]

12:2.t: When, then, after the time of Zechariah in the time of the Macedonian Empire was the Temple burnt? There was no such time. For after its burning by the Babylonians, it was not burned again till in the time of Titus and Vespasian, the Roman Emperors, it was utterly destroyed by fire, and it is in relation to this that the prophet summons the ancient rulers of the nation in a figure to mourn and weep, when he says: "Let the pine weep because the cedar is fallen, because the great ones are in great misery. Let the oaks of Bashan weep, because the wood that is planted is torn down: a voice of shepherds that lament, because their greatness is in misery." Then truly Jerusalem was as a portico shaken by all nations around it, and there was a force encircling Judaea, and their venerated Temple and its Holy Place is even to-day a stone trodden under the feet of all nations, and all that mock are mocked according to the prophecy.
12:2.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 4

12:2.t: This Creator, then, and Lord of the universe testifies that he will make Jerusalem a lintel of drunkenness for all the peoples round about, so that whoever touches its threshold may be made drunk and fall, or else the lintel itself may fall upon the one by whom it is touched. But Judah too, when Jerusalem is besieged, is captured by the nations, and passing into their fellowship he will be compelled to besiege his own mother city.

Concerning the Church it can be interpreted thus: that all the persecutors who have fought against the house of the Lord are made drunk with that cup which Jeremiah gives to all the nations to drink, so that they drink and are drunk, and fall, and vomit, and go mad. I know that in the time of persecution many of our own were compelled to fight against the Church; but whoever wishes to lift this weight will indeed lift it, and will bear it up in his hands for the wrath of the Lord by which he chastises sinners; yet he himself will not go unpunished, since the sword of God fights against him. For the stone of burden, which we have rendered as best we could, the Seventy translated: A stone trodden down by all the nations. Everyone who treads it down — or her, that is, Jerusalem —, mocking shall mock. Its sense is plain: that in both ways Jerusalem is to be trodden down both by hostile nations and by persecutors, and is to be mocked at the pleasure of those who mock. But the former sense is better and truer. […]

12:3.t: And not only will the Lord make Jerusalem like a lintel of drunkenness for all the peoples; he will also make her like a stone of burden for all the peoples, and whoever tries to lift it will be torn with gashing. For all the kingdoms of the earth will be gathered against Jerusalem. It is the custom in the cities of Palestine, and to this day the old practice is kept throughout all Judea, that in villages, towns and forts round stones of very great weight are set, on which young men are accustomed to exercise themselves; and they lift them according to the variety of their strength, some up to the knees, some up to the navel, others to the shoulders and the head, some above the crown of the head, with arms held straight and hands joined, raising the weight and showing the greatness of their strength. On the citadel of the Athenians, beside the statue of Minerva, I saw a bronze sphere of very great weight, which I, because of the weakness of my poor body, could scarcely move. […]

12:4.t: On that day, says the Lord, I will strike every horse with astonishment, and its rider with madness; and upon the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and every horse of the peoples I will strike with blindness. LXX: On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will strike every horse with astonishment, and its rider with madness; but upon the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and all the horses of the peoples I will strike with blindness. At that time — for this is what 'day' signifies —, when Jerusalem shall have been besieged, so that Judah too is compelled to besiege her, the Lord will strike, both carnally and spiritually, all the horses of the adversaries with astonishment, so that all who see that they have been struck are astonished, and their riders, under the pressure of the greatness of their ills, will be turned to madness; […]

12:5.t: And the chiefs of Judah shall say in their heart: Let the inhabitants of Jerusalem be strengthened for me in the Lord of hosts, their God. LXX: And the tribunes — that is, οἱ χιλίαρχοι —, of Judah shall say in their hearts: We shall find for ourselves those who dwell in Jerusalem in the Lord Almighty, their God. When the Lord has opened his eyes upon Judah, and has struck all the horses of the nations with blindness, the chiefs of Judah, of whom it was said above: But Judah too shall be in the siege against Jerusalem, will make vows in their hearts, since they will not dare to speak freely, that Jerusalem may conquer, and that Judah, conquered along with the enemies, may conquer along with his fellow citizens. […]

12:6.t: On that day I will make the chiefs of Judah like a furnace of fire among wood, and like a torch of fire in hay; and they shall devour to the right and to the left all the peoples round about; and Jerusalem shall be inhabited again in her own place, in Jerusalem. And the Lord shall save the tents of Judah, as in the beginning, so that the house of David may not glory magnificently, and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem against Judah. LXX: On that day I will make the tribunes of Judah like a firebrand among wood, and like hay of fire in stubble; and they shall devour on the right and on the left all the peoples of the Lord round about, and Jerusalem shall be inhabited still in herself; and the Lord shall save the tents of Judah, as from the beginning, so that the glory of the house of David may not be magnified, and the exaltation of the inhabitants of Jerusalem over Judah. […]

Let us say that, in the time of the Church's persecution, the chiefs and tribunes of the Christian name, of whom we spoke above, when the Lord has restored peace to Jerusalem and has slain the adversary with the spirit of his mouth, will be like a furnace of fire among wood, to devour the unfruitful trees, and like torches in stubble, so that whatever has no grain, and is carried about by every wind of doctrine, may be given over to burning. And the chiefs of Judah and the tribunes, he says, shall devour to the right and to the left those who were unwilling to walk in the middle of the road, who do not know that ὑπερβολὰς (excesses) belong to κακίας (vice); whence the people of God promises: we will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left, we will walk in the straight way. The right way is stinginess, which the Greeks call φειδολίαν; the left, extravagance; the middle and straight way, frugality.

All, then, who are on the right way, to whom it is said: Do not be overly just, and on the left, who hear: The ways that are on the left are perverse, the devouring flame shall consume; and when the adversaries have been destroyed and removed, Jerusalem, that is, the Church, will again receive her former glory; and she will be in her own state, and the tents of Judah will be saved, the gatherings of Christians scattered throughout the whole world, from which, as from tents and tabernacles, we long to go to the house that is not made with hands, and to the heavenly Jerusalem. And it is for this reason that the tents of the common people, and of all who are reckoned by the Christian name and are counted among the crowd, receive peace first, while the princes of the churches are besieged and put to flight, so that the masters and teachers may in no way think that peace was restored to the Churches by their own teaching and wisdom, but by the help of the Lord.

And of the holy apostles and evangelists Christ somewhere spoke by one of the prophets: "And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will make the heads of the thousands of Judaea like a firebrand among wood, and like a fiery lamp among reeds; and they shall devour on the right hand and on the left all the nations round about." For, so to speak, like fire they ate up all the nations, and fed upon the whole earth, kindling all its inhabitants, who as I said were cold, and had suffered the death of ignorance and sin.
12:6.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

12:7.t: Let them restore too the cities and towns, and the farms and villages of the tribe of Judah, which had been plundered and laid waste, as they had been before they were laid waste; and let the royal house, and the renowned and magnificent men of the tribe of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem in no way glory against the tribe of Judah, that it is ruled by their command and governed by their counsel; but let them know that the victory on both sides is the Lord's. Whether these things according to the history have been done or are yet to come, we leave the truth of the matter to the judgment of the Lord, and to his saints, who have received from him the spirit of wisdom and truth.

12:8.t: On that day the Lord shall shield the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and he who has stumbled among them on that day shall be as David. And the house of David as God, as the angel of the Lord in their sight. LXX: And it shall be on that day, the Lord shall shield the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and he who is weak among them on that day shall be as the house of David; and the house of David as the house of God, and the angel of the Lord in their sight. When Judah obtains the victory, and the Lord restores its tents as they had been from the beginning, so that the royal house may in no way glory against the people, on that day and at that time the Lord — by whose help Judah shall devour its adversaries on the right and on the left — shall shield also the besieged of Jerusalem, and all things shall be changed into such great happiness and blessedness that he who was thought the most worthless shall be as the royal house; […]

12:9.t: Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be moved. And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven, and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn (24, 29—30ᵃ). Since we consider that greater themes here come under discussion than lie within the grasp of human understanding — even of those who have advanced in wisdom far beyond others — let us come and examine the passage: first inquiring into those things which can readily be admitted for an exposition of the Gospel text, as though the Lord Himself were prophesying in it; and afterward we shall look for what the truth of these words may be according to those who judge that there is something deeper and more subtle in the words, keeping to the sequence of the moral traditions in these matters as well, in the same manner as above. […]

Nevertheless, when these things have thus been done, there shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven, and then the tribes of the earth shall mourn.
